deep-time.geology.text: The Indian plate was part of Gondwana until it broke away about 100 million years ago and moved north at about 20 cm a year. Its collision with Asia, from as early as 55 million years ago, built the Himalayas, which still rise by up to nearly 10 mm a year at Nanga Parbat.
deep-time.geology.kid: India used to be joined to lands far to the south. It broke off, drifted north and crashed into Asia. The crash pushed up the Himalayas, and they are still getting higher.

deep-time.climate.text: As it drifted, India crossed from far southern latitudes to the tropics; today the plate straddles the equator. The monsoon that now rules its climate, from June to September each year, is one of the oldest weather patterns known, yet is still only partly understood.
deep-time.climate.kid: As India drifted north it passed through hot and cool parts of the world. Today its weather is ruled by the monsoon, the great rains that come every year from June to September.

deep-time.life.text: Rocks of the subcontinent record its passengers. Rajasaurus, a meat-eating dinosaur, lived in the Narmada region in the Late Cretaceous. Vasuki, a snake 11 to 15 metres long, and Indohyus, a fox-sized relative of whales, lived in the Eocene. Apes called Sivapithecus lived here 12 million years ago.
deep-time.life.kid: Amazing animals once lived in India: a meat-eating dinosaur called Rajasaurus, a giant snake as long as a bus, a little animal related to whales, and later some early apes.

deep-time.extinctions.text: The Deccan Traps erupted between about 66.3 and 65.6 million years ago, across the time of the mass extinction that ended the age of dinosaurs. Some scientists have argued the eruptions' gases played a major part. Most now hold that the Chicxulub asteroid impact was the primary cause.
deep-time.extinctions.kid: When the dinosaurs died out, huge volcanoes were erupting in India. Some scientists think the volcanoes helped to kill them. Most think a giant rock from space was the main cause.

deep-time.oceans.text: North of drifting India lay the Tethys Ocean, the predecessor of the modern Indian Ocean. India's separation from Madagascar began 88 million years ago, and for a long time it was an island continent surrounded by sea.
deep-time.oceans.kid: While India drifted north it was an island with ocean all around it. The sea ahead of it was called the Tethys. It closed up as India reached Asia.

deep-time.cosmos.text: The subcontinent carries scars from space. Lonar Lake in Maharashtra fills a crater made by a meteorite, dated to about 52,000 years ago by some analyses and 570,000 by a disputed one. The much larger Dhala structure in Madhya Pradesh was formed by an asteroid impact.
deep-time.cosmos.kid: Rocks from space have hit India. One made the round hole that Lonar Lake now fills. Another, much bigger and much older, left a mark in Madhya Pradesh.

early-humans.power.text: Nothing survives to show how the small bands of the Old and Middle Stone Age organised themselves, who led them or how decisions were made. Stone tools and bones do not record it.
early-humans.power.kid: We do not know who was in charge in the Stone Age, or whether anyone was. Stone tools cannot tell us.

early-humans.war.text: There is no clear evidence of organised fighting between groups in the South Asian Stone Age. The later paintings at Bhimbetka that show warriors on horseback come from a much later time.
early-humans.war.kid: We have no sign that Stone Age people in India fought wars. Pictures of warriors on horses were painted much later.

early-humans.trade.text: The retrieved record says nothing reliable about exchange between Stone Age groups in South Asia. Any trade there was has left too little trace to describe.
early-humans.trade.kid: We do not know if Stone Age people here swapped things with other groups. Too little is left to tell.

early-humans.work.text: Work meant making tools and finding food. From about 2.5 million to 300,000 years ago people here made stone tools of the Acheulean and Soanian industries. The oldest tools at Attirampakkam, near Chennai, are dated to 1.5 million years ago.
early-humans.work.kid: The main jobs in the Stone Age were finding food and making tools from stone. Stone tools found near Chennai are one and a half million years old.

early-humans.food.text: For almost all of this era people lived as hunter-gatherers. Cut marks on fossil bone from the Himalayan foothills, 2.6 million years old, suggest very early scavenging of meat. Farming and settled life came only with the Neolithic, from about 7000 BCE.
early-humans.food.kid: Stone Age people did not farm. They hunted animals and gathered wild plants. Farming began only about 9,000 years ago.

early-humans.daily.text: People sheltered under rock overhangs such as those at Bhimbetka in central India, which hold the earliest traces of human life in India and were used across the Old and Middle Stone Ages.
early-humans.daily.kid: Many Stone Age people lived in the shelter of overhanging rocks. At Bhimbetka in central India, people used the same rock shelters for thousands and thousands of years.

early-humans.science.text: Stone Age people must have known their plants, animals, seasons and stone, but nothing they knew was written down, and the retrieved record does not let us describe it.
early-humans.science.kid: Stone Age people knew a great deal about animals, plants and stone. But they did not write, so we cannot say exactly what they knew.

early-humans.medicine.text: No evidence in the retrieved record shows how the sick and injured were cared for in the South Asian Stone Age.
early-humans.medicine.kid: We do not know how Stone Age people here looked after the sick. No evidence has been found.

early-humans.technology.text: Technology is the one thing that survives. Heavy Acheulean tools give way over time to smaller ones. At Jwalapuram in Andhra Pradesh, stone tools lie both under and over the ash of the Toba eruption of about 74,000 BC, showing that tool-makers lived there before and after it.
early-humans.technology.kid: Stone tools are almost all that is left of these people. At one place in southern India, tools lie both under and on top of a layer of ash from a giant volcano that erupted 76,000 years ago.

early-humans.religion.text: What Stone Age people believed is unknown. The paintings at Bhimbetka show animals, dancing and hunting, but what they meant to their makers cannot be recovered.
early-humans.religion.kid: We do not know what Stone Age people believed. Their paintings show animals and dancing, but we cannot ask the painters what they meant.

early-humans.arts.text: The earliest cave paintings at Bhimbetka are dated to 10,000 BCE. They show animals and early evidence of dance and hunting. In the Edakkal caves of Kerala, rock carvings are believed to date to at least 6,000 BCE.
early-humans.arts.kid: About 12,000 years ago people painted animals, hunters and dancers on the rock walls at Bhimbetka. In Kerala, others carved pictures into cave walls.

early-humans.language.text: Nothing is known of the languages spoken in South Asia in the Stone Age. Speech leaves no trace until writing, which lay many thousands of years in the future.
early-humans.language.kid: Stone Age people talked to each other, but we have no idea what their languages sounded like. Nobody could write yet.

early-humans.nature.text: These people lived through the ice ages of the Pleistocene, which ended 11,700 years ago, and through the Toba eruption of about 74,000 BC, whose ash fell across the subcontinent. A Middle Stone Age followed the end of the last glacial period.
early-humans.nature.kid: Stone Age people in India lived through ice ages and a giant volcanic eruption that covered the land in ash.

early-humans.movement.text: South Asia was reached early: signs of hominin activity in the Siwalik Hills go back 2.6 million years, which places the region closer to the centre of early human evolution than was once thought.
early-humans.movement.kid: Very early humans reached South Asia a very long time ago. Signs of them in the hills below the Himalaya are 2.6 million years old.

early-humans.women.text: The retrieved record cannot tell us how the lives of women and men differed in the Stone Age of South Asia. Tools and bones rarely show who used them.
early-humans.women.kid: We cannot tell how the lives of women and men were different in the Stone Age. Stone tools do not say who used them.

neolithic.power.text: Early farming villages such as Mehrgarh have left no sign of kings or governments. How these communities ran their affairs is not known.
neolithic.power.kid: The first farming villages had no kings that we know of. We cannot say how people made decisions together.

neolithic.war.text: The retrieved record gives no evidence of warfare among the first farmers of South Asia.
neolithic.war.kid: We have found no signs of war among India's first farmers.

neolithic.trade.text: Mehrgarh stood near the Bolan Pass, a natural route between the Indus plain and the highlands to the west, and its farming shows links with the Near East. Long-distance exchange in stones such as lapis lazuli is clear by the time of the later Indus colony at Shortugai.
neolithic.trade.kid: The first farmers lived near a mountain pass that travellers used. Later, the Indus people fetched a blue stone called lapis lazuli from far away in Afghanistan.

neolithic.work.text: Work changed completely: fields to tend, herds to keep, pots to make. Mehrgarh is one of the earliest sites in South Asia with evidence of farming and herding. At Lahuradewa in the Ganges plain is the oldest evidence of ceramics in the subcontinent.
neolithic.work.kid: When people began to farm, they had new jobs: sowing and harvesting, looking after animals and making clay pots.

neolithic.food.text: At Mehrgarh, from about 7000 BCE, people grew domesticated wheat and kept herd animals; the earliest evidence of cattle herding in South Asia comes from there. Wheat was also found at Burzahom in Kashmir and at Chirand on the Ganga.
neolithic.food.kid: The first farmers grew wheat and kept cattle. Now people could store food instead of searching for it every day.

neolithic.daily.text: Farming brought settled life. The earliest settlement at Mehrgarh was a small farming village. At Chirand in Bihar, villages were built one on top of another from 2500 BC, through the Neolithic, Chalcolithic and Iron Ages.
neolithic.daily.kid: Farmers stayed in one place and built villages. Some villages were lived in for so long that they slowly grew into mounds.

neolithic.science.text: Breeding crops and animals took generations of close observation, but the first farmers left no record of how they understood what they were doing.
neolithic.science.kid: The first farmers learned by careful watching which seeds and animals were best. But they left nothing written to tell us how they thought about it.

neolithic.medicine.text: Early Neolithic Mehrgarh has the oldest evidence anywhere for the drilling of human teeth in a living person, announced in the journal Nature in 2006. Archaeologists studying remains from the site concluded that its people practised a form of early dentistry.
neolithic.medicine.kid: The oldest signs of dentistry anywhere come from Mehrgarh. In the early farming age, someone there drilled holes in the teeth of living people.

neolithic.technology.text: Pottery is the era's new technology: Lahuradewa has the oldest in the subcontinent. Later came metal. The Ahar–Banas culture of Rajasthan, from about 3000 BCE, was Chalcolithic, a culture of the Copper Age.
neolithic.technology.kid: Farmers invented pottery to store and cook food. Later, people in Rajasthan learned to make things from copper.

neolithic.religion.text: What the first farmers believed is unknown. Without writing, their ideas about the world cannot be recovered from the retrieved evidence.
neolithic.religion.kid: We do not know what the first farmers believed about the world.

neolithic.arts.text: Rock art continued into the farming age. The Edakkal caves in Kerala hold carvings believed to date to at least 6,000 BCE. At Kupgal in Karnataka, thousands of petroglyphs date to the Neolithic or even earlier, some on rocks that ring when struck.
neolithic.arts.kid: People went on carving pictures into rock. At one place in Karnataka there are thousands of carvings, and some of the rocks ring like gongs when you hit them.

neolithic.language.text: Nothing is known of the languages of South Asia's first farmers. They left no writing.
neolithic.language.kid: We do not know what languages the first farmers spoke.

neolithic.nature.text: The Neolithic began after the last glacial period had ended and the climate had warmed. Farmers began to reshape the land with fields and herds.
neolithic.nature.kid: After the last ice age the weather grew warmer. Farmers began to change the land by clearing fields and grazing animals.

neolithic.movement.text: How farming reached South Asia is debated. Mehrgarh's wheat, pottery and herd animals resemble those of the Near Eastern Neolithic, and some scholars see a "cultural continuum" from eastern Mesopotamia to the western Indus valley.
neolithic.movement.kid: Did farming arrive from the west, or begin here too? Experts still argue. The wheat and animals at Mehrgarh look like those of the first farmers of the Near East.

neolithic.women.text: The oldest ceramic figurines in South Asia come from Mehrgarh. Many are of women; later ones were painted and given varied hairstyles and ornaments. What they meant is unknown, and they cannot tell us how farming changed women's lives.
neolithic.women.kid: The people of Mehrgarh made little clay figures of women, with fancy hairstyles and ornaments. We do not know what the figures were for.

indus.power.text: The Indus cities were planned on grids with shared drains, which implies authority. Yet there is no conclusive evidence of palaces or temples, and the cities are remarkable for their apparent, if relative, egalitarianism. Who governed them is unknown.
indus.power.kid: Somebody planned the Indus cities very carefully. But no king's palace has been found. Nobody knows who was in charge.

indus.war.text: The retrieved record offers no clear account of warfare in the Indus cities. Unlike Egypt and Mesopotamia, they have left no monuments boasting of conquest.
indus.war.kid: We know very little about fighting in the Indus cities. They left no pictures of kings winning battles.

indus.trade.text: Trade networks tied a huge area together. Copper came from Rajasthan and from as far as Oman; lapis lazuli from near the trading colony of Shortugai on the Oxus. Inscribed Indus objects have been found as far away as Mesopotamia.
indus.trade.kid: The Indus people were great traders. They fetched copper and blue stones from far away, and their seals have been found in Mesopotamia, in today's Iraq.

indus.work.text: Indus craftspeople made beads from imported stones and used standardised weights and stamp seals, most only two or three centimetres across. Goods probably moved in bullock carts and small flat-bottomed river boats.
indus.work.kid: Indus craftspeople made beads, weights and little seals. Goods were probably carried in ox carts and river boats.

indus.food.text: Before the cities rose, villagers of the region had already domesticated peas, sesame, dates and cotton, and the water buffalo. The civilisation flourished on the alluvial plain of the Indus and along rivers fed by the monsoon.
indus.food.kid: Indus farmers grew peas, sesame and dates, and kept water buffalo. Their fields lay on rich river mud.

indus.daily.text: Most houses at Mohenjo-daro were of fired brick around a courtyard, with water from wells. Several had a washing platform and a toilet flushed with a jar of water into a shared brick drain. Children played with terracotta animals and people with dice.
indus.daily.kid: Indus families lived in brick houses with wells and even toilets. Children had toy animals made of clay, and people played with dice.

sources.title: Sanitation of the Indus Valley Civilisation

indus.science.text: The cities were laid out on a grid, their bricks fired, their weights standardised. That takes measurement and shared rules, though no Indus text explaining them can be read.
indus.science.kid: The Indus people measured carefully. Their streets were straight and their weights were the same in every city.

indus.medicine.text: The Indus cities had the first known urban sanitation, which must have protected health. But nothing in the retrieved record describes Indus healing or medicine.
indus.medicine.kid: Clean water and drains kept the Indus cities healthier. But we know nothing about their doctors or medicines.

sources.title: Sanitation of the Indus Valley Civilisation

indus.technology.text: The Indus cities had water supply and sanitation devices that are the first known of their kind: wells, covered drains with inspection holes, and at Mohenjo-daro a brick bath 12 metres long made watertight with gypsum plaster and bitumen.
indus.technology.kid: The Indus people were brilliant with water. They built wells, covered drains, and a big brick pool sealed with tar so that it did not leak.

sources.title: Sanitation of the Indus Valley Civilisation

indus.religion.text: With no readable texts, Indus religion is guesswork. Most scholars think the Great Bath was used for rites of purification. A seal from Mohenjo-daro shows a seated figure, possibly three-headed. There is no conclusive evidence of temples.
indus.religion.kid: We cannot read what the Indus people wrote, so we can only guess at their religion. A big pool may have been used for holy bathing.

indus.arts.text: Two small sculptures are famous. The Dancing Girl, a bronze 10.5 cm tall, was made by lost-wax casting between about 2300 and 1750 BC. The Priest-King, in steatite, dates to around 2000–1900 BC and is the best-known stone sculpture of the civilisation.
indus.arts.kid: Indus artists made small, lively sculptures. The most famous are a bronze girl with bangles up her arm and a stone man with a beard.

indus.language.text: The Indus script has not been deciphered. Over 400 distinct signs are known from about 4,000 inscribed objects, but most inscriptions are extremely short and there is no bilingual text. Whether the signs record a language at all is still argued.
indus.language.kid: The Indus people left signs on seals and pots. More than 400 different signs are known, but nobody can read them.

indus.nature.text: The cities depended on rivers and rain. Mohenjo-daro stood on a ridge in the flood plain of the Indus. Earthquakes repeatedly struck Dholavira, including a severe one around 2600 BCE. From about 1900 BCE the civilisation declined.
indus.nature.kid: The Indus cities needed their rivers. Floods and earthquakes were always a danger. After about 1900 BCE the cities slowly emptied.

indus.movement.text: The civilisation spread over an area larger than ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia combined: from Sutkagan Dor near the Iranian border to Shortugai in northern Afghanistan and Lothal in Gujarat.
indus.movement.kid: Indus towns were spread over a huge area, from the border of Iran to Afghanistan and Gujarat.

indus.women.text: Women appear in Indus art: the bronze Dancing Girl, standing with one hand on her hip, and many terracotta female figurines. What these images meant, and what women's lives were like, the unread script cannot tell us.
indus.women.kid: Indus artists often made figures of women, like the famous Dancing Girl. But we cannot read their writing, so we know little about women's lives.

vedic.power.text: Early Vedic society, centred in the Punjab, was organised into tribes, not kingdoms. In the Middle Vedic period, about 1200 to 900 BCE, the Kuru kingdom emerged as a union of tribes, and the Brahmanical ideology took shape there.
vedic.power.kid: At first the Vedic people lived in tribes. Later some tribes joined together and formed the first kingdoms of northern India.

vedic.war.text: The Kuru kingdom was a union of the Bharata and Puru tribes. Tribal unions and rivalries shaped the age, though the Vedic texts are religious poetry, not chronicles, and battles in them are hard to date.
vedic.war.kid: Vedic tribes sometimes fought and sometimes joined together. The old poems mention battles, but it is hard to know exactly when they happened.

vedic.trade.text: The retrieved record has little to say about trade in the Vedic period. Wealth was counted mainly in cattle, and cities, markets and coins came later.
vedic.trade.kid: We know little about trade in Vedic times. People counted their wealth in cows, and there were no coins yet.

vedic.work.text: The early Vedic people lived mainly by herding. After about 1200–1000 BCE, as they spread to the western Ganges Plain, iron tools allowed forests to be cleared and a more settled, farming way of life took over.
vedic.work.kid: The Vedic people began as herders of cattle. Later, with iron tools, they cleared forests and became farmers.

vedic.food.text: A pastoral way of life sustained the early Vedic tribes. With iron tools and cleared land, agriculture became the main source of food on the Ganges Plain.
vedic.food.kid: At first the Vedic people lived mostly on what their cattle gave them. Later they grew crops in new fields.

vedic.daily.text: Life moved from the camps of herders to farming villages. The villages of the western Ganges plain in the Iron Age are known to archaeologists by their Painted Grey Ware pottery, dated from about 1200 to 600 BCE.
vedic.daily.kid: Vedic families settled down in farming villages. Archaeologists recognise these villages by their grey pots with painted patterns.

vedic.science.text: Keeping long sacred texts exact without writing demanded a science of sound and grammar. At the end of the period, between the 6th and 4th centuries BCE, Panini's Ashtadhyayi described the Sanskrit language in a rigorous grammar.
vedic.science.kid: To remember their long poems perfectly, Vedic scholars studied sounds and words very carefully. One of them, Panini, wrote a famous book of grammar.

vedic.medicine.text: The Atharvaveda, the fourth Veda and a late addition to the others, has been called "the procedures for everyday life". Its first books include poems for healing: spells against illnesses thought to be caused by demons, and potions made from herbs used as medicine.
vedic.medicine.kid: One of the Vedas, the Atharvaveda, contains healing spells and tells of medicines made from herbs.

vedic.technology.text: Iron is the era's great change: iron tools let farmers clear the forests of the Ganges Plain. Wheeled vehicles were already old. At Sinauli, Bronze Age vehicles with solid disk wheels have been excavated.
vedic.technology.kid: The big new thing in Vedic times was iron. Iron axes and ploughs helped people to clear forests and farm.

vedic.religion.text: The Vedas, composed between about 1500 and 900 BCE, are liturgical texts: hymns and formulas for ritual. They formed the basis of the Brahmanical ideology that developed in the Kuru kingdom.
vedic.religion.kid: The Vedas are very old hymns and prayers used in religious ceremonies. They are the oldest holy texts of Hinduism.

vedic.arts.text: The art of this age was verbal. The Vedas are poetry, composed and passed on by voice with great precision for centuries before they were written down.
vedic.arts.kid: The great art of Vedic times was poetry, spoken and sung from memory.

vedic.language.text: The Vedas were composed in an Old Indo-Aryan language and transmitted orally with precision. Panini's grammar, the Ashtadhyayi, later described a form of the Sanskrit language.
vedic.language.kid: The Vedas were made in an old form of Sanskrit and learned by heart, word for word, for hundreds of years.

vedic.nature.text: The Vedic age reshaped the land. From about 1200–1000 BCE, with iron tools, the forests of the western Ganges Plain were cleared for fields.
vedic.nature.kid: In Vedic times people cut down great forests along the river Ganges to make fields.

vedic.movement.text: Speakers of an Old Indo-Aryan language migrated into the north-west of the subcontinent early in this period. Around 1200–1000 BCE their culture spread east to the western Ganges Plain. Further east, Greater Magadha had a related but non-Vedic culture.
vedic.movement.kid: The people who composed the Vedas came into north-western India and later moved east along the river Ganges.

vedic.women.text: The Vedic texts were composed and passed on by priests, yet women thinkers appear in them. In the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, Gargi Vachaknavi takes part in a philosophical debate held by King Janaka of Videha and challenges the sage Yajnavalkya with questions about the soul.
vedic.women.kid: One old text tells of a wise woman, Gargi, who took part in a great debate at a king's court and asked the hardest questions.

mahajanapadas.power.text: From the sixth to the fourth century BCE, sixteen great states stretched across northern India, from Gandhara in the north-west to Anga in the east. Most were monarchies; two were most probably aristocratic republics. Magadha overshadowed, conquered and absorbed the others, and under the Nandas built a more centralised administration.
mahajanapadas.power.kid: Northern India was divided into sixteen big states. Most had kings, but a few were run by councils of nobles. One state, Magadha, grew stronger and swallowed up the rest.

mahajanapadas.war.text: Magadha grew by conquest: King Ajatashatru fought a war against the Vajjika League, and Magadha came to include most of Bihar and Bengal. In the north-west, Alexander the Great invaded in 327 BC and defeated King Porus at the Hydaspes in 326 BC, possibly the Macedonians' most costly battle.
mahajanapadas.war.kid: Magadha conquered its neighbours one by one. Far to the north-west, Alexander the Great marched in and beat King Porus in a hard battle beside a river.

sources.title: Indian campaign of Alexander the Great

mahajanapadas.trade.text: Coins appear: punch-marked pieces of irregular shape, dating from about the 6th century BC and found over most of the subcontinent. Cities such as Kosambi were trading centres on the Ganges Plain, and the route now called the Grand Trunk Road has linked South and Central Asia for at least 2,500 years.
mahajanapadas.trade.kid: People began to use coins, little pieces of metal stamped with marks. Traders travelled a great road that ran right across northern India.

mahajanapadas.work.text: In ancient India, traders, merchants and artisans formed associations called shreni, usually one for each occupation. A shreni was largely self-governing, acted as an economic body and, within limits, as a first court for its own members. The word is commonly translated as "guild".
mahajanapadas.work.kid: People who did the same job, such as merchants or craft workers, joined together in groups called shreni. A shreni made its own rules and settled its members' quarrels.

mahajanapadas.daily.text: After about 500 BCE new towns and cities arose on the Ganges plain: the "second urbanisation", long after the Indus cities. Their elites used a glossy black luxury pottery. Rajgir, capital of Magadha before Pataliputra, was ringed by a stone wall 40 kilometres long.
mahajanapadas.daily.kid: Cities grew up again in India, this time along the river Ganges. One of them, Rajgir, was guarded by a stone wall 40 kilometres long.

mahajanapadas.medicine.text: Jivaka, personal physician to the Buddha and to King Bimbisara, lived at Rajagriha, today's Rajgir, in the 5th century BCE. Accounts of him in early Buddhist texts made him a model healer, still honoured by traditional healers in several Asian countries.
mahajanapadas.medicine.kid: Jivaka was a famous doctor who lived about 2,500 years ago. He was the doctor of the Buddha and of a king. Healers in several Asian countries still honour him.

mahajanapadas.technology.text: This was an urban Iron Age. Potters made Northern Black Polished Ware, a burnished luxury ware that peaked about 500–300 BCE. Coins were stamped with punches. Builders raised long stone fortifications such as the wall of Rajgir, one of the few surviving structures in India older than the Mauryas.
mahajanapadas.technology.kid: People of this time used iron tools, made shiny black pottery, stamped the first coins and built huge stone walls around their cities.

mahajanapadas.religion.text: An age of seekers. Wandering ascetics called shramanas formed new spiritual movements. The Buddha, who lived in the eastern Ganges plain in the 6th or 5th century BCE, founded Buddhism; Mahavira is honoured by Jains as the 24th Tirthankara; the Ajivikas taught absolute fate. The Upanishads turned Vedic thought towards meditation and philosophy.
mahajanapadas.religion.kid: Many people at this time asked big questions about life. Two great teachers, the Buddha and Mahavira, lived then. Buddhism and Jainism grew from their teaching.

mahajanapadas.arts.text: The age is remembered in stories and verse. The Jatakas are a huge body of tales about the earlier births of the Buddha, in human and animal form; they were later carved on the railings and gateways of stupas. The Therigatha collects short poems said to be by early Buddhist nuns.
mahajanapadas.arts.kid: The Jataka tales tell of the Buddha's earlier lives, sometimes as a person and sometimes as an animal. Later, artists carved them in stone.

mahajanapadas.language.text: Panini described Sanskrit in a rigorous grammar between the 6th and 4th centuries BCE. Speech was changing: Pali, later the sacred language of Theravada Buddhism, is a Middle Indo-Aryan language. In Gandhara, the Kharosthi script developed between the 5th and 3rd centuries BCE.
mahajanapadas.language.kid: The scholar Panini wrote down the rules of Sanskrit. Ordinary people spoke newer languages such as Pali. In the north-west, people began to use a script called Kharosthi.

mahajanapadas.nature.text: Rivers decided where power sat. Magadha was based in the eastern Ganges Plain. Its later capital, Pataliputra, began as a small fort near the Ganges about 490 BCE and grew at the meeting of the Son and the Ganges, chosen for its central position.
mahajanapadas.nature.kid: The strongest kingdom, Magadha, lay along the river Ganges. Its capital was built where two big rivers meet.

mahajanapadas.movement.text: The north-west was drawn into empires from the west. Around 535 BCE Cyrus the Great of Persia annexed a large region west of the Indus, and Darius continued the campaign. In 327–325 BC Alexander's Macedonians took Gandhara and the Indus Valley, going beyond the old Persian frontier.
mahajanapadas.movement.kid: Armies from the west marched into north-western India: first the Persians, and two hundred years later the army of Alexander the Great.

sources.title: Achaemenid conquest of the Indus Valley
Indian campaign of Alexander the Great

mahajanapadas.women.text: In Buddhist tradition, Mahapajapati Gotami, the Buddha's foster-mother, was the first woman to seek ordination and became the first Buddhist nun. The Therigatha, "Verses of the Elder Nuns", collects 73 poems said to have been spoken by early nuns, some dating to the late third century BCE.
mahajanapadas.women.kid: The Buddha's foster-mother asked to become a nun, and tradition says she was the first. Poems said to be by early Buddhist nuns still survive.

maurya.power.text: Chandragupta Maurya founded the empire around 320 BCE from its base in Magadha; it lasted, in loose-knit fashion, until 185 BCE. Ashoka, the third ruler, reigned from about 268 to 232 BCE over a large part of the subcontinent.
maurya.power.kid: Chandragupta Maurya built an empire that covered a large part of India. The third emperor, Ashoka, is one of the most famous rulers in Indian history.

maurya.war.text: Between 305 and 303 BCE Chandragupta faced Seleucus I, who had crossed the Indus; it ended in a marriage alliance, with territory for Chandragupta and war elephants for Seleucus. About 261 BCE Ashoka conquered Kalinga. His own edict records 100,000 killed and 150,000 deported, and his deep remorse.
maurya.war.kid: Ashoka conquered the kingdom of Kalinga in a terrible war. Afterwards he wrote that 100,000 people had been killed, and that he felt deep sorrow for it.

maurya.trade.text: The Mauryan economy was helped by coinage and by the use of writing, which may have made more intricate business dealings possible. The route now called the Grand Trunk Road linked the Ganges plain with Central Asia, and Greek envoys such as Megasthenes travelled to the capital.
maurya.trade.kid: Coins and writing made buying and selling easier in the Mauryan empire. A great road joined the east of India to the north-west and the lands beyond.

maurya.work.text: According to Tim Dyson, the Mauryan period saw the consolidation of caste among the Indo-Aryan people settled in the Gangetic plain. It was also an age of skilled stone-workers, who cut and raised monolithic pillars, and of the scribes and carvers who set the emperor's edicts on rock.
maurya.work.kid: Under the Mauryas, caste, the sorting of people into groups by birth, grew stronger. Skilled stone workers carved huge pillars, each from a single piece of rock.

maurya.food.text: Settled agriculture in the fertile eastern Gangetic plain was profitable. There was planning for bad years: the Sohgaura copper plate, written in Brahmi of the Mauryan period, describes three granaries set up for the public in times of famine and scarcity.
maurya.food.kid: Farms along the Ganges grew plenty of food. Storehouses of grain were set up to feed people when there was a famine.

maurya.daily.text: The capital, Pataliputra, beside modern Patna, was one of the largest cities in the world in Ashoka's reign, with perhaps 150,000 to 400,000 people. Megasthenes reported it as ten miles long and one and three-quarter miles wide. Excavations found large fortification walls reinforced with timber.
maurya.daily.kid: The capital city, Pataliputra, was one of the biggest cities in the world. A Greek visitor said it was ten miles long, and it had walls strengthened with wood.

maurya.science.text: Pingala, a scholar, grammarian and mathematician of about the 3rd or 2nd century BCE, wrote the Chandahshastra, a treatise on prosody, the metres of verse. Writing itself comes into view: Brahmi appears as a fully developed script in the 3rd century BCE.
maurya.science.kid: A scholar named Pingala studied the rhythms of poetry and was a mathematician too. And from this time we can see Indian writing, in a script called Brahmi.

maurya.medicine.text: One of Ashoka's edicts states that he established two kinds of medical treatment, for people and for cattle, everywhere in his dominions and among his neighbours, from the Cholas and Pandyas in the south to the lands of the Greek king it calls Antiyoka.
maurya.medicine.kid: Ashoka had his orders carved on rocks. One says that he set up medical care for people and for animals all across his empire and beyond.

maurya.technology.text: Mauryan masons gave sandstone and granite a very smooth, shiny surface, the "Mauryan polish" seen on Ashoka's pillars and in the Barabar caves. The pillars are monoliths. In semi-arid Kathiawar, Chandragupta commissioned an artificial lake, Sudarshana, which later kings renovated.
maurya.technology.kid: Mauryan stone workers could polish stone until it was smooth and shiny. They cut tall pillars from single blocks of stone, and made a lake to store water in a dry land.

maurya.religion.text: Ashoka's edicts provide the first tangible evidence of Buddhism. They tell of his conversion, his efforts to spread dhamma, and his moral precepts. The oldest surviving rock-cut caves in India, in the Barabar hills, date from this empire. Tradition says the monk Mahinda carried Buddhism to Sri Lanka.
maurya.religion.kid: Ashoka became a Buddhist and tried to spread good behaviour, which he called dhamma. He had his messages carved on rocks and pillars for everyone to see.

maurya.arts.text: The Lion Capital, set up at Sarnath about 250 BCE, has four life-sized lions back to back above a drum carved with wheels, a lion, an elephant, a bull and a galloping horse. In 1947 it became the model for India's state emblem. The Didarganj Yakshi is one of the finest very early Indian stone statues, though its date is debated.
maurya.arts.kid: The most famous Mauryan sculpture shows four lions standing back to back. It once sat on top of a pillar at Sarnath. Today it is the model for India's state emblem.

maurya.language.text: Ashoka's edicts in central and eastern India were written in Magadhi Prakrit in the Brahmi script; in the north-west he used Prakrit in the Kharoshthi script, and also Greek and Aramaic. Brahmi's descendants, the Brahmic scripts, are still used across South and Southeast Asia.
maurya.language.kid: Ashoka's messages were written in the languages people spoke, and even in Greek in the far north-west. The script he used, Brahmi, is the ancestor of many scripts used in Asia today.

maurya.nature.text: Ashoka's edicts forbade the killing of wild animals and the destruction of forests; one lists protected creatures from parrots and wild geese to tortoises, porcupines and the rhinoceros. Some modern environmental historians see him as an early embodiment of that ethos.
maurya.nature.kid: Ashoka made rules to protect animals. His list included parrots, geese, tortoises, bats and the rhinoceros. He also told people not to destroy forests.

maurya.movement.text: People and ideas moved along the empire's routes. Megasthenes came from the Seleucid court to Pataliputra as ambassador and left the first Western written description of India. According to Sri Lankan tradition, Mahinda and his sister Sanghamitta carried Buddhism to Sri Lanka.
maurya.movement.kid: A Greek ambassador, Megasthenes, came to the Mauryan court and wrote a book about India. Buddhist monks and nuns travelled from India to Sri Lanka.

maurya.women.text: The Mauryan period saw declining rights for women in the mainstream Indo-Aryan-speaking regions of India, alongside the consolidation of caste. One woman remembered from the age is Sanghamitta, a Buddhist nun believed in Sri Lankan tradition to be Ashoka's daughter, who went to Sri Lanka to spread the Buddha's teaching.
maurya.women.kid: Many women had fewer rights in this time than before. One famous woman was Sanghamitta, a Buddhist nun who travelled to Sri Lanka to teach.

mahajanapadas.food.text: The Central Ganges Plain, where Magadha gained prominence, was the area of the earliest known cultivation of rice in South Asia. After 500 BCE the same plain carried the era's new states and their large fortified cities.
mahajanapadas.food.kid: The land along the middle Ganges is where rice was first grown in South Asia. In this era, big new cities grew up on that same rich land.

mahajanapadas.science.text: Ritual drove early mathematics. The Shulba Sutras, named after the measuring cord, contain the geometry needed to build fire altars; the oldest were possibly compiled between about 800 and 500 BCE. Panini's grammar of Sanskrit, from between the 6th and 4th centuries BCE, is as rigorous in its own field.
mahajanapadas.science.kid: To build altars of exactly the right shape, priests worked out rules of geometry using stretched cords. These rules are some of India's oldest mathematics.

post-maurya.power.text: After the Mauryas, power was shared out. Pushyamitra took the throne of Magadha and founded the Shunga Empire, about 187 to 75 BCE. The Satavahanas ruled from the late 2nd century BCE to the early 3rd century CE. The Kushan Empire, about 30 to 375 CE, reached its height under Kanishka.
post-maurya.power.kid: When the Mauryan empire ended, India split into many kingdoms. Among them were the Shungas, the Satavahanas and the Kushans, whose greatest emperor was Kanishka.

post-maurya.war.text: Kingdoms were won by force. Pushyamitra took the throne of Magadha from the Mauryas. In western India the Saka rulers called Western Satraps and the Satavahanas fought over territory: the satrap Nahapana ruled former Satavahana lands, and Gautamiputra Satakarni appears to have defeated him, since Nahapana's coins were overstruck with his name.
post-maurya.war.kid: Kings fought over land. In western India, the Satavahana king Gautamiputra beat a rival ruler and stamped his own name over the loser's coins.

post-maurya.trade.text: Sea trade with the Roman world grew after Augustus conquered Egypt in 30 BC. The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, written in Greek in the first century by a merchant of Roman Egypt, describes the Indian port of Barygaza at length. Inland, traders crossing the Western Ghats paid tolls at the Naneghat pass.
post-maurya.trade.kid: Ships sailed between India and the Roman Empire. A Greek-speaking merchant wrote a guide for sailors that describes Indian ports. Traders crossing the mountains had to pay a toll.

post-maurya.work.text: Craft workers organised in guilds and left their names in stone. An inscription on the Southern Gateway of the Great Stupa at Sanchi records that the ivory-workers of nearby Vidisha did the carving, a dedication by their guild. It has been suggested that ivory carvers made the gateway's stone reliefs.
post-maurya.work.kid: Craft workers belonged to guilds. On a gateway at Sanchi, a carved message says that the ivory carvers of a nearby town did the work.

post-maurya.food.text: A first-century Greek sailing guide describes the country behind the port of Barygaza as fertile, "yielding wheat and rice and sesame oil and clarified butter", and cotton. The medical compendium of Charaka, of about the same age, has sections on the importance of diet.
post-maurya.food.kid: A visitor 2,000 years ago wrote that western India grew wheat, rice and sesame, and made ghee and cotton cloth.

post-maurya.daily.text: Everyday feeling survives in the Gaha Sattasai, a collection of love poems in Maharashtri Prakrit attributed to a king named Hala, though probably by many hands. Most are frank monologues by a married woman or an unmarried girl, telling her longings to a friend, her mother or a relative.
post-maurya.daily.kid: A book of short love poems from this time lets us hear ordinary voices. In most of them a woman or a girl tells a friend or her mother how she feels.

post-maurya.science.text: The Naneghat inscriptions, attributed to a Satavahana queen, include the world's oldest numeration symbols for 2, 4, 6, 7 and 9 that resemble modern numerals, closest to those of the modern Nagari and Hindu-Arabic scripts.
post-maurya.science.kid: In a cave by a mountain pass, an old carving has number signs for 2, 4, 6, 7 and 9 that look like the numbers we use today. They are the oldest such signs known.

post-maurya.medicine.text: The Charaka Samhita, a Sanskrit text of Ayurveda attributed to Charaka of about the 1st–2nd century CE, sets out theories of physiology, diagnosis, anatomy and the three humours of the body. It stresses diet, hygiene, prevention and medical education, and the teamwork of physician, nurse and patient.
post-maurya.medicine.kid: A famous book of Indian medicine, the Charaka Samhita, comes from this time. It says that good food, cleanliness and preventing illness matter, and that doctor, nurse and patient must work together.

post-maurya.technology.text: Around 150 CE the Saka ruler Rudradaman had a rock near Junagadh inscribed with the history of the Sudarshana Lake: its water management and irrigation conduits from the time of Chandragupta Maurya to his own. In Maharashtra, builders cut Buddhist shrines out of the living rock, as at Karla.
post-maurya.technology.kid: A ruler named Rudradaman had the story of a great lake carved on a rock: who made it and who kept it working for more than 400 years. Other builders carved whole halls out of solid rock.

post-maurya.religion.text: Faiths multiplied and mixed. Around 113 BCE a Greek ambassador, Heliodorus, set up a pillar at Vidisha venerating Vasudeva, among the first archaeological evidence of Vaishnavism. A Buddhist text records a dialogue between the sage Nagasena and the Indo-Greek king Menander. Kharavela of Kalinga was a Jain king. Nagarjuna, about 150–250 CE, founded the Madhyamaka school of Mahayana Buddhism.
post-maurya.religion.kid: Many religions lived side by side. A Greek ambassador put up a pillar to an Indian god. A Greek king is said to have questioned a Buddhist monk. And a great Buddhist thinker, Nagarjuna, lived in southern India.

post-maurya.arts.text: Sculpture flourished. Gandhara's Greco-Buddhist art is believed to have produced the first images of the Buddha in human form, and it flowered under the Kushans; Mathura was another great centre from the 2nd century BCE. At Sanchi, four carved gateways were added in the 1st century BCE. The Natya Shastra, a treatise on the performing arts, took shape.
post-maurya.arts.kid: Artists began to make statues of the Buddha as a person for the first time. At Sanchi, carvers covered four stone gateways with pictures. A book called the Natya Shastra set out the rules for performing on stage.

post-maurya.language.text: Languages met on coins and rocks. Indo-Greek kings combined Greek and Indian languages on their coins, and the Kushans at first used Greek for administration. Prakrit was the language of the Hathigumpha inscription and of the Gaha Sattasai's poems, while Rudradaman's inscription of about 150 CE is in Sanskrit prose.
post-maurya.language.kid: Some coins of this time carry both Greek and an Indian language. Kings had messages carved in Prakrit, the everyday speech, and later in Sanskrit too.

post-maurya.nature.text: Geography shaped the age's routes. The Western Ghats stand between the Konkan coast and the Deccan plateau, and trade funnelled through passes such as Naneghat. In semi-arid Kathiawar, rulers kept up an artificial lake across the centuries. Sailors chose the favourable times of year that the Periplus records.
post-maurya.nature.kid: Mountains, dry lands and winds shaped life. Traders crossed the Western Ghats by mountain passes. In dry Kathiawar, rulers looked after a lake. Sailors waited for the right season to cross the sea.

post-maurya.movement.text: Peoples and ideas crossed the north-west in both directions. The Yuezhi, at first based in Bactria, formed the Kushan Empire, which spread over much of today's Afghanistan, Pakistan and northern India. By way of the Kushans, Mahayana Buddhism entered Han China along the Silk Road in the 1st or 2nd century CE.
post-maurya.movement.kid: New peoples came into India from Central Asia and built the Kushan empire. Going the other way, Buddhist monks carried their religion along the Silk Road to China.

post-maurya.women.text: The Naneghat cave inscriptions are attributed to a queen of the Satavahana dynasty, likely the queen mother, who sponsored the cave after her husband's death; they tell of their life together and of her son, the new king. Women's voices also fill the love poems of the Gaha Sattasai.
post-maurya.women.kid: A Satavahana queen had a long message carved in a cave by a mountain pass, telling about her husband and her son, the new king.

sangam.power.text: Three dynasties, the Chera, Chola and Pandya, dominated the politics of Tamilakam, the ancient Tamil country; they are remembered as the Three Crowned Kings. Around them were lesser chieftains such as Vel Pari and Athiyaman, known through the poets they befriended.
sangam.power.kid: Three royal families, the Cheras, Cholas and Pandyas, ruled the Tamil lands of the far south. They are called the Three Crowned Kings.

sangam.war.text: The Purananuru gathers 400 heroic poems about kings, wars and public life. The Chola king Karikala is credited with conquests across Tamilakam. Hero stones, memorials to those who died honourably in battle, were set up in India from the second half of the first millennium BCE.
sangam.war.kid: Many Sangam poems are about brave kings and battles. People set up carved stones to remember heroes who died fighting.

sangam.trade.text: The south traded with Rome. Muziris, a port on the Malabar Coast near the mouth of the Periyar, is celebrated in Tamil poems and Graeco-Roman texts. At Arikamedu near Pondicherry, digs found amphorae, Roman lamps and glassware. Inland, Kodumanal lay midway on the route between Muziris and the port of Puhar.
sangam.trade.kid: Ships from the Roman world came to ports in southern India. At one port, archaeologists have dug up Roman jars, lamps and glass.

sangam.work.text: At Kodumanal, in today's Erode district, people were highly skilled craft workers who specialised in making beads and high-quality iron. Poetry was a craft too: the Purananuru alone preserves the work of 157 poets.
sangam.work.kid: In the town of Kodumanal, skilled workers made beads and very good iron. Poets were important people, and the names of more than a hundred of them are remembered.

sangam.food.text: Farming in the Chola country depended on the Kaveri. Karikala is credited with building flood banks along the river, and the Kallanai, a stone dam, was built across it to divert water to the delta and boost irrigation. It is the oldest water-regulating structure in India still in use.
sangam.food.kid: Farmers in the south needed river water for their fields. A stone dam built across the river Kaveri in ancient times still sends water to farms today.

sangam.daily.text: Keezhadi, in Sivaganga district of Tamil Nadu, is a settlement of the Sangam period now being excavated. One expert dated its remains to between the 6th and 3rd centuries BCE, though some of the dating has been questioned. The Sangam poems, too, offer a window into ancient Tamil life.
sangam.daily.kid: At Keezhadi in Tamil Nadu, archaeologists are digging up a settlement from this time. The old Tamil poems also tell us how people lived.

sangam.science.text: The Sangam poems are about love and war, and the retrieved sources do not describe the scientific knowledge of the early Tamil kingdoms. What can be shown from the ground, such as steel-making, is described under technology.
sangam.science.kid: The old Tamil poems are about love and war, not science. So we cannot say much about what people then knew of numbers or the stars.

sangam.medicine.text: Siddha medicine of South India is described as one of the oldest systems of medicine in India, but the retrieved sources give no dated evidence for how the sick were treated in the Sangam age itself.
sangam.medicine.kid: Southern India has a very old kind of medicine called Siddha. But we have no dated record of how doctors worked in Sangam times.

sangam.technology.text: Wootz steel, a crucible steel with a high carbon content, was a pioneering alloy developed in southern India in the mid-1st millennium BC. It was produced in ancient Tamil Nadu, exported as cakes of steel, traded westward, and later associated with the making of Damascus steel.
sangam.technology.kid: Smiths in southern India invented a very good steel called wootz. It was sold to faraway lands.

sangam.religion.text: Most Sangam poetry is about love and war, but shorter poems such as those of the Paripaatal are more religious and praise Vishnu and Murugan. Tamil tradition links the literature's legendary beginnings to Shiva and his son Murugan.
sangam.religion.kid: Most of the old Tamil poems are about love and war. But some are hymns of praise to gods such as Murugan and Vishnu.

sangam.arts.text: Sangam literature is the earliest known literature of South India: poems of love (akam) and war (puram), which most scholars place between about 300 BCE and 300 CE. Love poems were sorted into modes tied to landscapes, such as mountains for union and forests for waiting.
sangam.arts.kid: The oldest poems of southern India were composed in Tamil about 2,000 years ago. Some are about love and some about war. In the love poems, each kind of landscape stands for a feeling.

sangam.language.text: The Tolkappiyam is the oldest surviving Tamil grammar and the oldest surviving long work of Tamil literature. Tamil was written in Tamil-Brahmi, a variant of the Brahmi script dated between the third century BCE and the first century CE, found on cave entrances, potsherds, coins, seals and rings.
sangam.language.kid: The oldest book of Tamil grammar comes from this age. People wrote Tamil in a script called Tamil-Brahmi, on pots, coins, rings and cave walls.

sangam.nature.text: Sangam poets read feeling into the land. Their love poetry is divided into seven modes, five of them tied to particular landscapes: among them kurinji, the mountains, linked with union, and mullai, the forests, linked with waiting.
sangam.nature.kid: Tamil poets loved the land. They gave each kind of country its own kind of love poem: mountains for lovers meeting, forests for waiting.

sangam.movement.text: The sea joined the Tamil country to its neighbours. Ellalan (235–161 BCE), of the Tamil Chola dynasty, captured the throne of Anuradhapura in Sri Lanka. At Arikamedu, the excavator Mortimer Wheeler concluded that Greek (Yavana) traders dealing with Rome kept a trading post for about two hundred years.
sangam.movement.kid: People crossed the sea in both directions. A Tamil ruler from the Chola family became king in Sri Lanka, and traders from the Roman world lived at a port in southern India.

sangam.women.text: Women were among the Sangam poets. At least 10 of the 157 poets of the Purananuru were women. One, Avvaiyar, wrote 59 of its poems and is said to have been on cordial terms with the chieftains Vel Pari and Athiyaman.
sangam.women.kid: Some Sangam poets were women. One of them, Avvaiyar, wrote 59 poems in one famous collection and was a friend of chiefs.

gupta.power.text: The Gupta Empire lasted from the mid 3rd to the mid 6th century CE and at its peak covered much of the northern subcontinent. Samudragupta, the second emperor, turned an inherited kingdom into a vast empire; Chandragupta II ruled from about 375 to about 415. Some historians call the period a Golden Age; others dispute it.
gupta.power.kid: The Gupta kings ruled for about 300 years, and at their strongest they held most of northern India. Some people call their time a golden age, though not all historians agree.

gupta.war.text: The Allahabad Pillar inscription, a eulogy by the courtier Harisena, credits Samudragupta with extensive military conquests. The empire later lost territory to its own former feudatories and to the Huna peoples, the Kidarites and Alchon Huns, invading from Central Asia; the Alchon invasion contributed to its fall.
gupta.war.kid: The Gupta king Samudragupta won many wars, and a poem carved on a pillar lists his victories. Later, invaders called the Huns helped to bring the empire down.

gupta.trade.text: The Guptas exported luxury goods such as silk, leather goods, fur, iron products, ivory, pearls and pepper from centres such as Nasik, Paithan, Pataliputra and Benares. Strong trade ties made the region a cultural centre that influenced kingdoms in India and Southeast Asia. Tamralipta was a port on the Bay of Bengal.
gupta.trade.kid: Gupta India sold silk, ivory, pearls, pepper and iron goods to other lands. Trade carried Indian ideas as far as Southeast Asia.

gupta.work.text: The empire's exports point to its trades: workers in silk, leather, iron, ivory and pearls. Eran, in central India, was one of the ancient mints, as the varied coins dug up there show. And smiths could forge an iron pillar weighing more than six tonnes.
gupta.work.kid: Gupta craft workers wove silk, carved ivory, worked leather and made coins. Their iron workers were skilled enough to make a pillar that weighs more than six tonnes.

gupta.food.text: The Chinese monk Faxian, who travelled in India in these years, reported that throughout the country people did not kill living creatures, drink intoxicating liquor, or eat onions or garlic. This is one Buddhist pilgrim's sweeping account, not a survey of what everyone ate.
gupta.food.kid: A Chinese visitor wrote that people in Gupta India did not kill animals, drink wine, or eat onions and garlic. He was a monk, and probably did not see how everybody lived.

gupta.daily.text: Faxian described a yearly festival: on the eighth day of the second month, a four-wheeled car carrying a four-storey structure of tied bamboo is drawn in a procession of images. Monks and lay people gather with singers and skilful musicians, offer flowers and incense, and keep lamps burning all night.
gupta.daily.kid: A Chinese visitor described a festival he saw. A tall bamboo tower on wheels was pulled through the streets, with music, flowers and lamps that burned all night.

gupta.science.text: Aryabhata (476–550 CE) was the first of the major mathematician-astronomers of India's classical age. His Aryabhatiya gives 3.1416 as an approximation of pi and includes a table of sines and quadratic equations. Varahamihira worked at Ujjain. The Bakhshali manuscript uses place-value numerals with a dot for zero; its dating is debated.
gupta.science.kid: The mathematician Aryabhata worked out the number pi very accurately, about 1,500 years ago. Indian mathematicians also wrote numbers in places, with a dot for zero.

gupta.medicine.text: The Bower Manuscript, written on birch bark in early Gupta script in the 5th or early 6th century, includes the oldest dated fragments of an Indian medical text, the Navanitaka. The Sushruta Samhita, built up in layers over centuries, has unique chapters on surgical training, instruments and procedures.
gupta.medicine.kid: Some of the oldest pages of Indian medical writing come from Gupta times, written on birch bark. Another old book, the Sushruta Samhita, explains how to train surgeons and what tools they need.

gupta.technology.text: The iron pillar now at Mehrauli in Delhi was made under Chandragupta II. It stands 7.21 metres high, is 41 centimetres across and weighs more than six tonnes, and the metal has a rust-resistant composition.
gupta.technology.kid: Gupta smiths made an iron pillar more than seven metres tall. It is about 1,600 years old and has hardly rusted.

gupta.religion.text: The Udayagiri Caves near Vidisha, devoted mainly to Vishnu and Shiva, hold some of the oldest surviving Hindu temples and iconography in India; the early 6th-century temple at Deogarh is one of the earliest Hindu stone temples still standing. Buddhism flourished too: Kumaragupta I founded the great monastery of Nalanda around 427 CE.
gupta.religion.kid: Some of the oldest Hindu temples still standing were built in Gupta times. A Gupta king also founded Nalanda, a great Buddhist monastery where monks came to study.

gupta.arts.text: Kalidasa, of the 4th–5th century, is often considered ancient India's greatest poet and playwright. The paintings and sculpture of the Ajanta Caves, finished by about 480 CE, are regarded as masterpieces of Buddhist art. Samudragupta's gold coins and inscriptions suggest that the emperor himself was a poet and played the veena.
gupta.arts.kid: The poet Kalidasa wrote plays and poems that are still loved. In the caves of Ajanta, artists painted beautiful pictures on the rock walls. One Gupta emperor played a stringed instrument called the veena.

gupta.language.text: Classical Sanskrit was the language of court and learning. Kalidasa wrote his plays and poems in it; Harisena composed Samudragupta's eulogy on the Allahabad Pillar; and the Amarakosha, a thesaurus whose formal title means "instruction concerning nouns and gender", organised its vocabulary.
gupta.language.kid: Poets and scholars of Gupta times wrote in Sanskrit. One scholar even made a book that lists Sanskrit words by their meaning, like a thesaurus.

gupta.nature.text: Nature fills the era's poetry. In Kalidasa's Meghaduta, the "Cloud Messenger", a banished nature spirit asks a cloud to carry a message of love to his wife. The poet tells the cloud not to miss the city of Ujjayini on its way, even if it must take a detour.
gupta.nature.kid: In a famous poem by Kalidasa, a lonely spirit asks a rain cloud to carry a message to his wife far away, and tells it which places to see on the way.

gupta.movement.text: Faxian, a Chinese Buddhist monk, set out at about the age of 60 and travelled on foot to India to collect scriptures, entering from the north-west and reaching Pataliputra. He sailed home by way of Sri Lanka; a violent storm drove his ship onto an island, probably Java. From the other direction, Huna peoples came in from Central Asia.
gupta.movement.kid: A Chinese monk named Faxian walked all the way to India when he was about 60, to find Buddhist books. He went home by sea and was nearly shipwrecked.

gupta.women.text: Prabhavatigupta, a Gupta princess and Vakataka queen, effectively ruled the Vakataka realm as regent from about 390 to 410 after her husband's death. A darker record is at Eran: an inscription of 510 CE there is the first epigraphic evidence of sati, the burning of a widow.
gupta.women.kid: A Gupta princess named Prabhavatigupta ruled a kingdom for about twenty years after her husband died. But life could be cruel for widows, as one stone inscription from 510 shows.

chola.power.text: The Chola Empire was a sea-going empire based in southern India, with dominions and influence overseas. Rajaraja I, who reigned from 985 to 1014, conquered southern India and the Anuradhapura kingdom of Sri Lanka; in 1000 he ordered a land survey. His son Rajendra I founded a new capital, Gangaikonda Cholapuram, about 1025.
chola.power.kid: The Chola kings of southern India ruled a great empire that reached across the sea. Rajaraja the Great and his son Rajendra were its most powerful kings.

chola.war.text: Rajaraja invaded Sri Lanka about 993, and the Cholas stayed for some three-quarters of a century. In 1025 Rajendra I sent a naval expedition against Srivijaya in Southeast Asia. The Cholas had no standing navy in the modern sense: trading ships carried the army overseas.
chola.war.kid: Chola armies crossed the sea to fight in Sri Lanka and in Southeast Asia. They had no special warships. Their soldiers travelled in trading ships.

chola.trade.text: Organised merchant guilds held great power between the 8th and 13th centuries. The Five Hundred Lords of Ayyavole, from Aihole, linked trading communities across Tamil Nadu, Karnataka and Andhra. Nagapattinam was an important Chola port, and the Cholas sent repeated embassies to China; Kulottunga I kept up contacts with Srivijaya, China and the Khmer Empire.
chola.trade.kid: Rich groups of merchants called guilds traded all over southern India and across the sea. The Chola kings sent messengers as far as China.

chola.work.text: Agriculture was the main occupation, and farming settlements were the foundation of the economy; above them were commercial towns called nagaram, whose artisans made goods for trade abroad. Chola kings saw temples as places of economic activity as well as worship. Even soldiers built: Rajaditya's army raised the dam of Veeranam Lake while in camp.
chola.work.kid: Most people in the Chola lands were farmers. In the towns, craft workers made things to sell. Soldiers once built a huge lake while they were waiting to fight.

chola.food.text: Farming fed the empire, and farming needed stored water. Veeranam Lake, made in the 10th century behind a dam 16 kilometres long, can hold about 1,465 million cubic feet of water. The ancient Kallanai dam on the Kaveri sent the river's water to the fields of the delta.
chola.food.kid: Chola farmers grew their food with water saved in giant man-made lakes. One of the lakes has a wall 16 kilometres long.

chola.daily.text: Temple inscriptions at Uthiramerur, south-west of Chennai, describe how a village governed itself. Executive powers were given to committees called variyams, and an inscription dated 919 CE sets out the rules for electing their members.
chola.daily.kid: In one Chola village, the rules for choosing the village committees were carved on the temple wall more than a thousand years ago. You can still read them there.

chola.science.text: The retrieved sources describe Chola temples, trade and government in detail but say little about scientific learning in the Chola lands. Their survey of land in 1000 shows careful measurement, but its methods are not described.
chola.science.kid: We know a lot about Chola temples and ships, but our sources say little about Chola science.

chola.medicine.text: Kundavai, the elder sister of Rajaraja I, built a hospital at Thanjavur, named after her father, and gave extensive lands for its upkeep.
chola.medicine.kid: A Chola princess, Kundavai, built a hospital in the city of Thanjavur and gave land to pay for it.

chola.technology.text: Rajaraja I built the Brihadisvara Temple at Thanjavur between 1003 and 1010 from granite; the tower above its shrine is one of the tallest in South India. Chola metalworkers cast bronzes of classic grace. Engineers built long dams to make lakes, one of which still supplies water to Chennai.
chola.technology.kid: Chola builders raised a giant temple of granite in only a few years. Their metalworkers made beautiful bronze statues, and their engineers made lakes that still hold water today.

chola.religion.text: The great Chola temples were dedicated to Shiva. The Tirumurai gathers twelve volumes of Tamil hymns to Shiva from the 6th to the 11th century, and the Periya Puranam tells the lives of the sixty-three Nayanar saints. Ramanuja was a leading teacher of Sri Vaishnavism. Princess Kundavai commissioned temples for Jain Tirthankaras, Vishnu and Shiva alike.
chola.religion.kid: The Chola kings built great temples to the god Shiva. Poets wrote hymns in Tamil, and stories were told of sixty-three saints. A Chola princess built temples for three different faiths.

chola.arts.text: From about 850 to 1250 the Cholas spent the wealth of their conquests on lasting stone temples and exquisite bronze sculpture. The best-known bronze form is Nataraja, Shiva as the divine cosmic dancer. Three of their temples are a World Heritage Site, the "Great Living Chola Temples".
chola.arts.kid: Chola artists made some of the most beautiful bronze statues in the world. The most famous shows the god Shiva dancing.

chola.language.text: Chola patronage produced some of the greatest works of Tamil literature. Kambar (1180–1250) wrote the Ramavataram, known as the Kambaramayanam, the Tamil version of the Ramayana. Hymns of the Tirumurai were compiled, and royal deeds were recorded in Tamil inscriptions.
chola.language.kid: Tamil poetry flourished under the Cholas. The poet Kambar retold the story of Rama in Tamil, and his poem is still famous.

chola.nature.text: The Cholas reshaped their landscape with water. Rajendra's capital was remarkable for its artificial lake. Veeranam Lake still fills when heavy rain in the Western Ghats sends water down the tributaries of the Kaveri.
chola.nature.kid: The Cholas changed the land by making lakes. One of their lakes still fills up when the rains fall on mountains far away.

chola.movement.text: Chola power reached far beyond India: expeditions to the Ganges, naval raids on the cities of Srivijaya on Sumatra, and repeated embassies to China. Rajendra's campaign strengthened Indian influence in Southeast Asia. Kulottunga I had relations with Cambodia, Srivijaya, Pagan in Burma, and China.
chola.movement.kid: Chola ships and soldiers travelled to Sri Lanka, Sumatra and beyond. Chola messengers went all the way to China.

chola.women.text: Royal women shaped the Chola world. Sembiyan Mahadevi, queen from 949 to 957, built numerous temples and gave generously to others over sixty years. Kundavai, sister of Rajaraja I, commissioned temples for three faiths and founded a hospital at Thanjavur.
chola.women.kid: Chola queens and princesses were great builders. Queen Sembiyan Mahadevi built temples for sixty years, and Princess Kundavai built a hospital.

early-medieval.power.text: No single empire held the subcontinent. Harsha ruled from Kannauj from 606 to 647. From 785 to 816 three dynasties, the Pratiharas, the Palas of Bengal and the Rashtrakutas, fought for Kannauj; the Pratiharas won. The Pala line began when the chiefs of Gauda elected Gopala. In the south, the Chalukyas ruled between the 6th and 12th centuries.
early-medieval.power.kid: India was divided among many strong kingdoms. Three of them fought for thirty years over one famous city, Kannauj. In Bengal, the chiefs chose their own king by election.

early-medieval.war.text: Between 711 and 713 the Umayyad Caliphate defeated the Chach dynasty and made Sindh a province. Mahmud of Ghazni, sultan from 998 to 1030, attacked Somnath in Gujarat in 1025. In 1192, at Tarain north of Delhi, the Ghurid forces of Muhammad Ghuri decisively defeated the Rajput confederacy of Prithviraj Chauhan.
early-medieval.war.kid: Armies came into India from the west: first Arabs into Sindh, then the raids of Mahmud of Ghazni. In 1192 Muhammad Ghuri beat the Rajput king Prithviraj Chauhan in a great battle near Delhi.

early-medieval.trade.text: About 849 CE the chieftain of Kollam, on the Kerala coast, issued a copper-plate grant conferring privileges on a Syrian Christian merchant named Maruvan Sapir Iso. Between the 8th and 13th centuries organised merchant guilds such as the Ainnurruvar held considerable power and influence.
early-medieval.trade.kid: A chief on the Kerala coast gave special rights to a Christian merchant from far away, and had them written on copper plates. Groups of merchants called guilds grew rich and strong.

early-medieval.work.text: Temples show the labour of the age. Archaeologists believe the Kailasa temple at Ellora was sculpted from a single rock; its top rises 32.6 metres above the court. At Khajuraho the Chandela dynasty built most of its temples between 885 and 1000, and 85 stood there by the 12th century.
early-medieval.work.kid: Stone workers built great temples. At Ellora they carved a whole temple out of one giant rock.

early-medieval.food.text: The Manasollasa, a Sanskrit encyclopedia composed in the early 12th century by the Chalukya king Someshvara III, who ruled in present-day Karnataka, includes chapters on food recipes and festivals, as well as on horticulture.
early-medieval.food.kid: A king of Karnataka wrote a huge book about nearly everything, almost 900 years ago. It even includes recipes for food.

early-medieval.daily.text: Chaturanga, a strategy board game first known from India around the seventh century, is by the prevailing view the common ancestor of chess. The Manasollasa describes games, perfumes, painting, dance and music. Xuanzang reported that children started school at seven, beginning with grammar.
early-medieval.daily.kid: People in India played a board game called chaturanga, which later turned into chess. A Chinese visitor wrote that children started school when they were seven.

early-medieval.science.text: Brahmagupta (c. 598–668) is credited as the first person to formalise zero as a number in mathematics. Bhaskara II wrote the Lilavati, a treatise on mathematics, in 1150. Al-Biruni, who accompanied Mahmud's campaigns, finished a great study of India, the Tarikh al-Hind, around 1030.
early-medieval.science.kid: The mathematician Brahmagupta was the first to treat zero as a real number with its own rules. Five hundred years later, Bhaskara wrote a famous maths book called the Lilavati.

early-medieval.medicine.text: Madhava-kara, a practitioner of the 7th or early 8th century, wrote the Madhava Nidana: 79 chapters listing diseases with their causes, symptoms and complications, including one on smallpox. The works linked to the name Vagbhata became some of the most influential in Ayurveda. Xuanzang listed medicine among the five fields of knowledge taught to the young.
early-medieval.medicine.kid: A doctor named Madhava wrote a book that lists diseases one by one, with their causes and signs. One chapter is about smallpox.

early-medieval.technology.text: Builders worked rock and water on a grand scale. The Kailasa temple is a megalith carved into a cliff. Rani ki Vav at Patan, an 11th-century stepwell, descends through seven levels of stairs. Bhojtal at Bhopal was made by an earthen dam across the Kolans River.
early-medieval.technology.kid: Builders carved a temple out of a cliff, dug a well with seven levels of steps going down to the water, and made a lake by building a dam of earth.

early-medieval.religion.text: The Bhakti movement of personal devotion began in the Tamil country in the 6th century, in the songs of the Alvars and Nayanars. Adi Shankara, in the 8th century, taught Advaita Vedanta. Buddhism flourished at monasteries such as Vikramashila, founded by the Pala king Dharmapala. At Khajuraho, Hindu and Jain temples stand together.
early-medieval.religion.kid: In southern India, poet-saints sang songs of love for God, and a new kind of worship called bhakti began. Great Buddhist monasteries in the east drew students from far away.

early-medieval.arts.text: Stone was the era's great medium: the 7th- and 8th-century monuments of Mahabalipuram on the Coromandel Coast, the Kailasa temple of Ellora, considered one of the most remarkable cave temples, and the Nagara-style temples of Khajuraho.
early-medieval.arts.kid: Artists of this time carved wonderful temples from stone, on the seashore at Mahabalipuram, inside a cliff at Ellora, and at Khajuraho.

early-medieval.language.text: Regional languages found their voice in literature. The Kavirajamarga of 850 is the earliest available work on poetics and grammar in Kannada. The Charyapada, mystical Buddhist songs compiled between about 1000 and 1200, is in late Apabhramsha. Sanskrit remained the language of learning: Kalhana wrote his chronicle of Kashmir's kings in it in the 12th century.
early-medieval.language.kid: People began to write books in the languages they spoke at home, such as Kannada. Sanskrit was still used for learning and history.

early-medieval.nature.text: Water was stored and honoured. Bhojtal, the lake at Bhopal made by damming the Kolans River, still supplies drinking water to about 40 per cent of the city's residents. Rani ki Vav was designed as an inverted temple symbolising the sanctity of water; it later silted over.
early-medieval.nature.kid: Water was precious. People made lakes and deep wells with steps. One well was built like an upside-down temple, to show that water is holy.

early-medieval.movement.text: Xuanzang travelled through the subcontinent from 629 to 645 and carried at least 657 Indian texts back to China. The Bengali teacher Atisha went to Sumatra and Tibet. A later Parsi narrative, written in 1599, tells how Zoroastrian refugees fled Iran after the Arab conquest and settled in India.
early-medieval.movement.kid: A Chinese monk, Xuanzang, spent sixteen years travelling to India and back and took hundreds of books home. Refugees from Iran settled in India and became the Parsi community.

early-medieval.women.text: Didda ruled Kashmir for decades: as regent for her son and grandsons from 958, and as sole monarch from 980 to 1003. Andal is the only woman among the twelve Alvars, the Tamil poet-saints of Vishnu. The stepwell Rani ki Vav is attributed to Udayamati, queen of the Chaulukya king Bhima I.
early-medieval.women.kid: Queen Didda ruled Kashmir for more than forty years. In the south, Andal was the only woman among twelve famous poet-saints.

delhi-sultanate.power.text: The Delhi Sultanate was established in 1206 and lasted more than three centuries under five dynasties: Mamluk, Khalji, Tughlaq, Sayyid and Lodi. It reached its greatest extent under the Tughlaqs. In 1327 Muhammad bin Tughluq ordered the capital moved to Daulatabad in the Deccan; in 1347 the Bahmani kingdom broke away there.
delhi-sultanate.power.kid: For more than 300 years, sultans ruled much of India from Delhi. Five families of sultans followed one another.

delhi-sultanate.war.text: The Mongols invaded the subcontinent repeatedly between 1221 and 1327; Alauddin Khalji fended off several invasions. Khalji and Tughlaq armies pushed deep into southern India. Timur sacked Delhi on 17 December 1398. On 21 April 1526 Babur's guns and cannon defeated Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat.
delhi-sultanate.war.kid: The sultans of Delhi fought off the Mongols many times. But in 1398 the conqueror Timur captured and robbed Delhi. In 1526 Babur beat the last sultan with cannons and guns.

delhi-sultanate.trade.text: The sultanate drew the subcontinent more closely into international Islamic social and economic networks. Alauddin Khalji imposed price controls. In the east, the Bengal Sultanate had a network of mint towns striking the taka and was linked by sea and land to Asia, Africa and Europe.
delhi-sultanate.trade.kid: Under the sultans, India traded more with the Muslim lands to the west. One sultan fixed the prices of goods. Bengal made its own coins and sent ships across the ocean.

delhi-sultanate.work.text: Army officers were paid through the iqta: a temporary grant of the tax revenue of a piece of land in place of a regular wage. In the villages, cloth-making changed: according to historians, the spinning wheel was introduced from Iran in this period, and the earliest clear Indian reference to one dates from 1350.
delhi-sultanate.work.kid: Soldiers were often paid with the taxes from a piece of land. Spinners got a new tool, the spinning wheel, for making thread.

delhi-sultanate.food.text: Sultans intervened in the food supply. Alauddin Khalji's changes covered revenues and price controls. Firuz Shah Tughlaq, sultan from 1351 to 1388, founded more than 300 villages and dug five major canals; he also laid out gardens.
delhi-sultanate.food.kid: The sultans tried to make sure there was enough food. One fixed prices. Another dug five big canals to bring water to the fields.

delhi-sultanate.daily.text: Ibn Battuta, the traveller and jurist from Morocco, wrote about his time at the court of Muhammad bin Tughluq. Under Firuz Shah, many rest houses for travellers, gardens and tombs were built.
delhi-sultanate.daily.kid: A traveller from Morocco, Ibn Battuta, lived at the sultan's court and wrote about what he saw. Rest houses were built along the roads for travellers.

delhi-sultanate.science.text: Far from Delhi, in Kerala, Madhava of Sangamagrama (c. 1340–1425) founded a school of astronomy and mathematics. He made pioneering contributions to the study of infinite series and was the first to use infinite-series approximations for a range of trigonometric functions.
delhi-sultanate.science.kid: In Kerala, the mathematician Madhava found a way to work out hard numbers by adding up an endless list of smaller and smaller pieces.

delhi-sultanate.medicine.text: Unani medicine, a Greco-Arabic system based on the four humours, arrived in India by the 12th century, carried by Muslim scholars, and took root there. It was influenced in turn by Indian and Chinese traditional systems.
delhi-sultanate.medicine.kid: Muslim scholars brought a kind of medicine called Unani to India. It began with the ideas of the ancient Greeks and is still practised in South Asia today.

delhi-sultanate.technology.text: The Sultanate period coincided with more use of mechanical technology in the subcontinent, including the spinning wheel. Firuz Shah's engineers dug major canals. At its very end came gunpowder: Panipat in 1526 was one of the earliest battles involving gunpowder arms on the subcontinent.
