delhi-sultanate.technology.kid: New machines arrived in India in this time, like the spinning wheel. At the end of the era came cannons and guns.

delhi-sultanate.religion.text: Sufi orders spread Islam's mystical side: Muin al-Din Chishti carried the Chishti order to Ajmer, and Nizamuddin Auliya (1238–1325) taught in Delhi. From the 15th century the Bhakti movement swept north India. Kabir's verses are honoured in several faiths. Guru Nanak (1469–1539) founded Sikhism.
delhi-sultanate.religion.kid: Muslim holy men called Sufis taught in India. The poet Kabir is honoured by Hindus, Sikhs and Sufis alike. Guru Nanak founded a new religion, Sikhism.

delhi-sultanate.arts.text: The Qutb Minar in Delhi, a minaret and victory tower with 399 steps, was mostly built between 1199 and 1220. A new Indo-Islamic architecture developed under the sultans. Amir Khusrau (1253–1325), singer, musician and court poet, is regarded as the "father of qawwali", a devotional form of singing.
delhi-sultanate.arts.kid: The sultans built the Qutb Minar, a very tall tower with 399 steps. The poet and musician Amir Khusrau is called the father of qawwali singing.

delhi-sultanate.language.text: The Sultanate's wider connections show in the development of the Hindustani language, whose two standard registers today are Hindi and Urdu, the latter Persianised and Arabised. Amir Khusrau wrote mainly in Persian but also in Hindavi and Punjabi; a verse vocabulary of Arabic, Persian and Hindavi words is often attributed to him.
delhi-sultanate.language.kid: In the sultans' time a new language grew up in north India. Today its two forms are called Hindi and Urdu. Poets at court wrote mostly in Persian.

delhi-sultanate.nature.text: Rulers began to redirect rivers. Firuz Shah Tughlaq built a canal joining the Sarasvati and Markanda rivers near Sirhind, built a palace complex at Hisar in 1354, and dug five major canals in all.
delhi-sultanate.nature.kid: One sultan dug canals to carry river water across the land, and planted gardens.

delhi-sultanate.movement.text: People arrived from every side. Mongol armies raided for a century. Travellers such as Ibn Battuta, born in Tangier, came to the sultan's court. In the far north-east, Sukaphaa, a Tai prince from Mong Mao, founded the Ahom kingdom in the Brahmaputra valley in 1228.
delhi-sultanate.movement.kid: Many people came to India in these years: Mongol raiders, travellers from Muslim lands, and a Tai prince who founded a kingdom in Assam.

delhi-sultanate.women.text: Razia ruled as Sultan of Delhi from 1236 to 1240, the first female Muslim ruler of the subcontinent; nobles who expected a figurehead deposed her when she asserted her power. Rudrama Devi reigned over the Kakatiya kingdom from 1262 to 1289. In Kashmir, Lalleshwari (c. 1320–1392) created a style of mystic poetry.
delhi-sultanate.women.kid: Razia was the only woman ever to rule as Sultan of Delhi. In the south, Queen Rudrama Devi ruled a kingdom for 27 years. In Kashmir, the poet Lal Ded made a new kind of poem.

vijayanagara.power.text: The Vijayanagara Empire was established in 1336 by the brothers Harihara I and Bukka Raya I and ruled much of southern India from its capital beside the Tungabhadra. It reached its political and cultural zenith under Krishnadevaraya, emperor from 1509 to 1529. The capital was abandoned in 1565.
vijayanagara.power.kid: Two brothers founded the Vijayanagara Empire in 1336. It ruled most of southern India for more than 200 years. Its greatest king was Krishnadevaraya.

vijayanagara.war.text: Vijayanagara fought repeatedly with the sultanates to its north. In 1520 it won a decisive victory over Bijapur at Raichur. On 23 January 1565 an alliance of the Deccan sultanates, with superior artillery tactics, defeated it at Talikota; a sultan's army camped in the capital for six months and the city was ruined.
vijayanagara.war.kid: Vijayanagara and the sultans of the Deccan fought many wars. In 1565 the sultans joined together and won a great battle. Afterwards the capital city was destroyed.

vijayanagara.trade.text: Paes, who came with traders from Portuguese Goa about 1520, listed the kingdom's seaports on the west coast, some with Portuguese trading posts, and described a busy market of precious stones in the capital. Horses were vital imports: Krishnadevaraya made a treaty with the Portuguese to stop the supply of horses to Bijapur. Fernão Nunes was himself a horse trader.
vijayanagara.trade.kid: Merchants from Portugal came to Vijayanagara to trade. They sold horses to the king and saw a market full of precious stones.

vijayanagara.work.text: Large-scale cotton production supplied the weaving centres of the empire's vibrant textile industry. Contemporary records and travellers' notes describe huge tanks constructed by labourers. Temple-building employed masons and sculptors across the south.
vijayanagara.work.kid: Many people in the empire grew cotton or wove cloth. Labourers dug huge tanks to hold water, and builders raised great temples.

vijayanagara.food.text: Wheat, sorghum, cotton and pulses grew in the semi-arid regions, while sugarcane and rice thrived where rain was plentiful. Betel leaves, areca nuts for chewing, and coconut were the principal cash crops. State-sponsored irrigation canals and reservoirs supported intense agriculture.
vijayanagara.food.kid: Farmers grew rice and sugarcane in wet places and wheat and sorghum in dry ones. They also grew coconuts and betel leaves to sell.

vijayanagara.daily.text: Persian and European travellers describe the capital as a prosperous, wealthy and grand city with numerous temples, farms and trading markets. To Paes it seemed comparable in size to Rome, with abundant vegetation, aqueducts and artificial lakes. By one estimate it was the world's second-largest city by 1500, after Beijing.
vijayanagara.daily.kid: Visitors said the city of Vijayanagara was as big as Rome, full of markets, temples, gardens and lakes. It may have been the second-biggest city in the world.

vijayanagara.science.text: On the Kerala coast, the school of astronomy and mathematics founded by Madhava continued. Nilakantha Somayaji (1444–1544) completed his Tantrasamgraha in 1500–1501, with a computational model in which the planets orbit the Sun and the Sun orbits the Earth. In the empire itself, court patronage encouraged writing on astronomy and mathematics.
vijayanagara.science.kid: In Kerala, the astronomer Nilakantha worked out a model of the sky in which the planets circle the Sun. He finished his great book in 1501.

sources.title: Kerala school of astronomy and mathematics

vijayanagara.medicine.text: Court patronage stimulated writing in Kannada, Telugu, Tamil and Sanskrit on topics that included medicine. Portuguese visitors described Krishnadevaraya as a commander who personally tended wounded soldiers. Beyond this, the retrieved sources give little detail of how medicine was practised in the empire.
vijayanagara.medicine.kid: Scholars at the court wrote books about medicine. Visitors said that King Krishnadevaraya himself looked after his wounded soldiers.

vijayanagara.technology.text: Water engineering was the empire's strength: state-sponsored canals and reservoirs, and the aqueducts and artificial lakes Paes saw in the capital; he also recorded advanced irrigation technology. In war, artillery mattered more and more, and the sultanates' better-integrated guns decided the battle of 1565.
vijayanagara.technology.kid: Vijayanagara's engineers built canals, lakes and stone water channels to bring water to the city and its fields.

vijayanagara.religion.text: Vijayanagara was a Hindu empire of monumental temple complexes; the Virupaksha temple at Hampi is still an active place of worship. Sayana, who died in 1387, wrote influential commentaries on the Vedas under its early kings. Purandara Dasa (c. 1470–1564) was a singer-saint of the Haridasa tradition.
vijayanagara.religion.kid: The kings of Vijayanagara built huge Hindu temples. One of them, at Hampi, is still used for worship today.

vijayanagara.arts.text: Vijayanagara builders added two features to the temples of the south: large halls with intricately carved pillars, and tall entrance towers. Purandara Dasa was one of the chief founders who shaped modern Carnatic music. Krishnadevaraya himself composed the Telugu epic Amuktamalyada, considered a masterpiece.
vijayanagara.arts.kid: Vijayanagara's builders made temples with tall gate towers and halls of carved pillars. The singer Purandara Dasa helped to shape the music of southern India.

vijayanagara.language.text: Court patronage stimulated literature in four languages: Kannada, Telugu, Tamil and Sanskrit. Krishnadevaraya's reign is regarded as a golden age of Telugu literature, and a body of Kannada writing runs from the 14th to the 16th century.
vijayanagara.language.kid: Writers at the Vijayanagara court wrote in four languages: Kannada, Telugu, Tamil and Sanskrit.

vijayanagara.nature.text: The capital stood on the banks of the Tungabhadra River, and its people stored the river's water and the rain in canals and reservoirs. What was grown depended on rainfall: dry-land crops in the semi-arid regions, rice and sugarcane in the rainy ones.
vijayanagara.nature.kid: The capital stood beside the river Tungabhadra. Much of the land around was dry, so people saved water in big tanks.

vijayanagara.movement.text: Visitors came by sea and land. Abd al-Razzaq, ambassador of the Timurid ruler of Persia, described Calicut and Vijayanagara. The Portuguese took Goa from Bijapur in 1510 and made it their main anchorage. Telugu-speaking Nayaks moved south to rule Madurai from about 1529.
vijayanagara.movement.kid: Travellers came to Vijayanagara from Persia and Portugal and wrote about what they saw. The Portuguese captured Goa in 1510.

vijayanagara.women.text: Women wrote some of the era's literature. Gangadevi was a 14th-century princess and Sanskrit poet. Tirumalamba, poet, musician and grammarian, composed a poem on the wedding of the emperor Achyuta. Molla, a potter's daughter of the 16th century, wrote a Telugu Ramayana.
vijayanagara.women.kid: Women wrote famous poems in Vijayanagara times. One was a princess, Gangadevi. Another, Molla, was the daughter of a potter and retold the story of Rama in Telugu.

mughal.power.text: The Mughal Empire was founded by Babur in 1526. Akbar, the third emperor, reigned from 1556 to 1605; under Aurangzeb, 1658 to 1707, it reached its greatest extent. Officers held a mansab, a numerical rank that fixed precedence and salary. By 1760 the empire was reduced to the region around Delhi, and it was formally dissolved after the Rebellion of 1857.
mughal.power.kid: The Mughal emperors ruled most of India for about 200 years. The greatest were Akbar and Aurangzeb. The last emperor lost his throne in 1857.

mughal.war.text: Babur's firearms and cannon won the empire at Panipat in 1526. Aurangzeb carried Mughal arms across nearly the entire subcontinent. In 1739 Nader Shah of Iran easily defeated the crumbling Mughal army at Karnal and sacked Delhi.
mughal.war.kid: The Mughals won India with cannons and guns. Two hundred years later, when the empire was weak, the king of Iran captured Delhi and carried away its treasures.

mughal.trade.text: Taxes were paid in a well-regulated silver currency, which drew peasants and artisans into larger markets; Sher Shah Suri had issued the first rupiya. Growing European demand for Indian goods brought wealth to the court. Bengal was a major exporter of silk and cotton textiles, steel and saltpetre.
mughal.trade.kid: Mughal India sold cotton cloth, silk and many other goods to the world, and was paid in silver. The rupee comes from this time.

mughal.work.text: Most people farmed, and taxes took well over half of a peasant cultivator's output. Bengal was globally prominent in textile manufacturing and shipbuilding, and its economy began to undergo proto-industrialisation. Great building projects, such as the Taj Mahal, completed between 1648 and 1653, employed craftsmen for decades.
mughal.work.kid: Most people were farmers, and they had to give more than half of what they grew as tax. In Bengal, many people wove cloth or built ships.

mughal.food.text: Farmers grew wheat, rice and barley, and by the mid-17th century two new crops from the Americas, maize and tobacco. In the court kitchens Indian and Persian cooking combined in Mughlai cuisine. But harvests could fail: after three failed crops, the Deccan famine of 1630–1632 killed, by a contemporary estimate, as many as 7.4 million people.
mughal.food.kid: Mughal cooks mixed Indian and Persian cooking and made new dishes that people still love. Farmers began to grow maize, which came from America. But when the rains failed, terrible famines followed.

mughal.daily.text: There was conspicuous consumption among the Mughal elite, who spent on painting, literature, textiles and architecture. Mughal miniatures show court life, hunting scenes and portraits. For peasants and artisans, a regulated silver currency opened the way into larger markets, though taxes were heavy.
mughal.daily.kid: Rich Mughal nobles spent their money on paintings, fine clothes and beautiful buildings. Ordinary farmers paid heavy taxes.

mughal.science.text: Mughal astronomers made advances in observational astronomy and produced astronomical tables, though there was little concern for theory. A new curriculum for the madrasas stressed the rational sciences. At Jaipur the Rajput king Sawai Jai Singh built the Jantar Mantar, 19 astronomical instruments completed in 1734, including the world's largest stone sundial.
mughal.science.kid: Astronomers watched the sky carefully. A king of Jaipur built giant instruments of stone to measure the Sun and stars, including the biggest stone sundial in the world.

mughal.medicine.text: A new madrasa curriculum introduced medicine among its subjects, alongside geometry and mathematics. Court scholars such as Fathullah Shirazi, who died in 1588–89, counted medicine among their many fields. Unani medicine, which had arrived with Muslim scholars centuries earlier, continued to be practised.
mughal.medicine.kid: Medicine was one of the subjects taught in Mughal schools, along with mathematics.

mughal.technology.text: Mughal India had a large shipbuilding industry, centred in Bengal. Fathullah Shirazi, a polymath at Akbar's court, was an inventor skilled in mechanics. Sher Shah Suri organised a postal system and extended the Grand Trunk Road from Chittagong in Bengal to Kabul.
mughal.technology.kid: Mughal India built many ships. A great road with a postal service ran from Bengal all the way to Kabul.

mughal.religion.text: Akbar followed a policy of religious tolerance and promulgated Din-i Ilahi, a creed drawn mainly from Islam and Hinduism with elements of Zoroastrianism and Christianity. Aurangzeb imposed the Fatawa-i Alamgiri, a code of Islamic law. In these years the Sikh scripture, the Guru Granth Sahib, took shape, and Tulsidas wrote of Rama.
mughal.religion.kid: The emperor Akbar respected many religions. A later emperor, Aurangzeb, ruled strictly by Islamic law. The holy book of the Sikhs was put together in this time.

mughal.arts.text: Shah Jahan commissioned the Taj Mahal, an ivory-white marble mausoleum on the Yamuna at Agra, in 1631. Mughal painting, a miniature style that grew out of Persian painting, took a new interest in realistic portraits. Akbar founded Fatehpur Sikri as his capital in 1571. Hindustani classical music developed, with instruments such as the sitar.
mughal.arts.kid: The Mughals built the Taj Mahal, one of the most beautiful buildings in the world. Their artists painted tiny, detailed pictures of people, animals and court life.

mughal.language.text: Persian was the language of administration: Abu'l Fazl wrote the Ain-i-Akbari, a detailed account of Akbar's government, in Persian between 1589 and 1596. Tulsidas wrote his Ramcharitmanas in Awadhi, the speech of ordinary people. Urdu, closely related to Hindi, is today an official language in India and the national language of Pakistan.
mughal.language.kid: The Mughal court wrote in Persian. The poet Tulsidas retold the story of Rama in Awadhi, a language that ordinary people spoke.

mughal.nature.text: The Mughals built gardens on the Persian charbagh plan, meant to represent an earthly paradise in which people live in harmony with nature. The court painter Ustad Mansur, who died in 1624, excelled at plants and animals and was the earliest artist to depict the dodo in colour. Drought could still bring catastrophe, as in 1630.
mughal.nature.kid: The Mughals loved gardens and built many of them. One court painter made careful pictures of animals and birds, including the dodo.

mughal.movement.text: Babur came as an invader in 1526; the name Mughal is the Indo-Persian form of "Mongol". European trading companies arrived by sea in growing numbers. Pilgrims left for Mecca, among them the princess Gulbadan Begum with other royal women. In 1739 Nader Shah's army came from Iran.
mughal.movement.kid: The first Mughals came to India as invaders. In their time, traders from Europe began to arrive by ship, and pilgrims travelled from India to Mecca.

mughal.women.text: Nur Jahan (1577–1645), wife of Jahangir, is considered by some historians to have been the real power behind the throne for more than a decade. Gulbadan Begum, Babur's daughter, wrote the Humayun-Nama. Jahanara Begum wrote a biography of a Sufi saint. In the Deccan, Chand Bibi served as regent of both Bijapur and Ahmednagar.
mughal.women.kid: The empress Nur Jahan helped to rule the empire. Princess Gulbadan wrote a history of her brother, the emperor Humayun. In the south, Chand Bibi ruled two kingdoms for young kings.

regional-powers.power.text: As Mughal power faded, regional states took its place. The Maratha Empire (1674–1818) became a confederacy: the Peshwa's realm and four major Maratha states under the nominal leadership of the Chhatrapati. The Nawabs of Bengal were independent in all but name. In the Punjab, Ranjit Singh captured Lahore in 1799 and founded the Sikh Empire.
regional-powers.power.kid: When the Mughal empire grew weak, new kingdoms rose: the Marathas in the west, the Sikhs in the Punjab, and others in Bengal, Mysore and Hyderabad.

regional-powers.war.text: On 14 January 1761 the Marathas met the invading Durrani army at Panipat, in the largest battle of the 18th century. In 1741 Travancore defeated the Dutch East India Company at Colachel. The Third Anglo-Maratha War of 1817–1819 left the British company in control of most of India; the Sikh Empire fell in 1849.
regional-powers.war.kid: These kingdoms fought each other and invaders from Afghanistan. In the end the British East India Company beat them one by one: the Marathas by 1819 and the Sikhs in 1849.

regional-powers.trade.text: The Marathas levied chauth, an annual tribute nominally of a quarter of revenue, on lands under nominal Mughal rule; it worked as protection money against their raids. At sea, the Maratha admiral Kanhoji Angre captured European East Indiamen and collected tolls. In Bengal, European trading posts multiplied at Murshidabad, Dhaka, Patna and Hugli.
regional-powers.trade.kid: The Marathas made other states pay them a quarter of their income to be left in peace. On the coast, a Maratha admiral stopped European ships and made them pay tolls.

regional-powers.work.text: War was a livelihood. Pindaris, irregular plunderers and foragers, followed the Mughal and then the Maratha armies. Ranjit Singh's army and government employed Sikhs, Muslims, Hindus and Europeans. In Mysore, Tipu Sultan's new land revenue system began the growth of the Mysore silk industry.
regional-powers.work.kid: Many men earned their living as soldiers. Ranjit Singh's army had Sikhs, Muslims, Hindus and Europeans in it. In Mysore, people began to make silk.

regional-powers.food.text: The chefs and gourmet cooks of the Nawabs of Awadh invented the dum style of cooking over a slow fire, still strongly associated with Lucknow. At the Golden Temple in Amritsar, the langar, a free kitchen run by the Sikh community, offers a vegetarian meal to every visitor without discrimination.
regional-powers.food.kid: Cooks in Lucknow invented a way of cooking food very slowly over a low fire. At the Golden Temple, a free kitchen feeds everyone who comes.

regional-powers.daily.text: Lavani, a combination of song and dance performed to the beat of the dholki drum, was popular in Maharashtra. Rulers such as Ahilyabai Holkar paid for the public spaces of daily life: bathing ghats on rivers, schools, and rest houses for travellers and pilgrims.
regional-powers.daily.kid: People in Maharashtra enjoyed lavani, lively songs and dances to the beat of a drum. Good rulers built riverside steps, schools and rest houses for travellers.

regional-powers.science.text: Sawai Jai Singh II (1688–1743), ruler of Amber and founder of Jaipur, commissioned observatories at several places in India and had Euclid's "Elements" translated into Sanskrit. His Jaipur observatory, completed in 1734, has 19 instruments.
regional-powers.science.kid: King Jai Singh of Jaipur loved astronomy. He built observatories in several cities and had a famous Greek book of geometry translated into Sanskrit.

regional-powers.medicine.text: Serfoji II, the last sovereign Maratha ruler of Thanjavur, who died in 1832, is remembered for his contributions to ophthalmology. Manuscripts record eye operations believed to have been performed by the king himself, and he is known to have carried a surgical kit.
regional-powers.medicine.kid: King Serfoji of Thanjavur was also an eye doctor. Records tell of eye operations that he is believed to have done himself.

regional-powers.technology.text: Mysore developed the first successful iron-cased rockets in the late 18th century under Hyder Ali, and his son Tipu Sultan was a pioneer of rocket artillery. The Maratha navy used small, manoeuvrable vessels called gallivats and grabs, suited to shallow coastal waters.
regional-powers.technology.kid: The army of Mysore used rockets with iron cases, the first of their kind in the world. The Marathas built small, fast warships for fighting near the coast.

regional-powers.religion.text: Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Sikh Guru, initiated the Khalsa in 1699, with its code of conduct and dress. The Golden Temple at Amritsar is Sikhism's holiest site; Ranjit Singh paid homage there after taking the city in 1802. Ahilyabai Holkar commissioned temples and pilgrim rest houses.
regional-powers.religion.kid: The tenth Sikh Guru founded the Khalsa, a community of Sikhs with its own rules and dress. The Golden Temple in Amritsar is the holiest place of the Sikhs.

regional-powers.arts.text: In the hill kingdoms of the lower Himalaya, Pahari miniature painting flourished from the early 17th to the mid 19th century; the Kangra style became prevalent from the mid 18th. In the south, Tyagaraja (1767–1847) and his contemporaries Syama Sastri and Muthuswami Dikshitar composed the core of Carnatic music.
regional-powers.arts.kid: Painters in the Himalayan hill kingdoms made delicate little paintings. In the south, the composer Tyagaraja wrote songs that musicians still perform.

regional-powers.language.text: Marathi was a language of government and history. It was written in the cursive Modi script as well as Devanagari. More than 200 bakhars, historical narratives in Marathi prose, were written between the 17th and 19th centuries, the most important chronicling the deeds of rulers.
regional-powers.language.kid: The Marathas wrote their letters and records in Marathi, in a fast joined-up script called Modi. They also wrote more than 200 histories in Marathi.

regional-powers.nature.text: In 1760 Hyder Ali of Mysore commissioned the garden at Bengaluru now called Lalbagh. It became a botanical garden responsible for introducing and propagating many ornamental plants and plants of economic value.
regional-powers.nature.kid: The ruler of Mysore made a great garden in Bengaluru in 1760. Many new plants were first grown in India there. You can still visit it.

regional-powers.movement.text: The Marathas, a Marathi-speaking warrior group from the western Deccan, carried their power far to the north, where in 1761 they met an army invading from Afghanistan. Europeans moved in too: French officers trained the army of Mysore, and Europeans served Ranjit Singh.
regional-powers.movement.kid: Maratha armies marched far from their home in western India. Soldiers from Afghanistan and officers from France also came to fight in India's wars.

regional-powers.women.text: Tarabai, daughter-in-law of Shivaji, was regent of the Maratha state from 1700 to 1708. Ahilyabai Holkar (1725–1795) ruled Indore. Chennamma, queen of Kittur, led armed resistance to the East India Company. Begum Samru, who began as a dancing girl, became ruler of the small principality of Sardhana.
regional-powers.women.kid: Several women ruled in these years. Tarabai led the Marathas, Ahilyabai Holkar ruled Indore, and Queen Chennamma of Kittur fought the British.

company.power.text: The East India Company, a joint-stock company founded in 1600 for Indian Ocean trade, became a ruler. Its rule is usually dated from 1757, when Robert Clive defeated the Nawab of Bengal at Plassey, helped by the betrayal of Mir Jafar. It took the right to collect Bengal's revenue, and later annexed princely states under the Doctrine of Lapse.
company.power.kid: A British trading company slowly took over India. It began as a group of merchants, but after winning a battle in Bengal in 1757 it became a government with its own army.

company.war.text: The Company's conquests met resistance from the start. Indian sepoys mutinied at Vellore on 10 July 1806. The Santals rose against the Company and the zamindari system on 30 June 1855. On 10 May 1857 a mutiny of sepoys at Meerut began the great rebellion of 1857–58.
company.war.kid: Many Indians fought against the Company. In 1857 Indian soldiers in its army rebelled, and a great uprising spread across northern India.

company.trade.text: The Company came for trade and stayed to tax. The capital amassed from Bengal after its conquest in 1757 helped to finance British industries such as textile manufacture. A number of historians point to colonisation as a major factor both in India's deindustrialisation and in Britain's Industrial Revolution.
company.trade.kid: The Company grew rich from India. Money from Bengal helped to pay for new factories in Britain, while many Indian craft workers lost their work.

sources.title: Economy of India under Company rule

company.work.text: Under the Permanent Settlement of 1793, land revenue in Bengal was fixed and collected by zamindars, who were treated as landlords. From 1834 the indenture system carried Indian workers to overseas colonies, more than 1.6 million in all; on the early voyages over 17 per cent died.
company.work.kid: In Bengal, farmers now had to pay rent to landlords called zamindars. Many poor workers were shipped across the sea to work on farms in faraway British colonies.

company.food.text: The Great Bengal famine struck Bengal and Bihar in 1769–70, soon after the Company gained the right to collect revenue there; it affected some 30 million people, about a third of the population. Later the Company built the Ganges Canal, from 1842 to 1854, to irrigate the land between the Ganges and the Yamuna.
company.food.kid: A terrible famine struck Bengal in 1770, soon after the Company took control. Later, a great canal was dug to bring water from the Ganges to farmers' fields.

company.daily.text: New things entered daily life. In 1853 the first passenger train carried 400 people in 14 carriages over the 34 kilometres from Bombay to Thane. The telegraph was first installed in 1851. Indian artists working for European patrons painted the plants and birds around them in the hybrid "Company style".
company.daily.kid: In 1853 the first passenger train in India ran from Bombay to Thane with 400 people on board. Messages began to travel by telegraph wire.

company.science.text: William Jones founded the Asiatic Society in Calcutta on 15 January 1784 for research into India and its neighbours. The Great Trigonometrical Survey, begun in 1802 by William Lambton and continued by George Everest, measured the subcontinent with scientific precision. Earlier, the 12-volume Hortus Malabaricus had recorded Kerala's plants, drawing on the herbalist Itty Achudan.
company.science.kid: Scientists measured the whole of India with great care, in a survey that took almost seventy years. Others studied its plants, languages and history.

company.medicine.text: The first cholera pandemic began near Calcutta in 1817 and spread across Asia to the Mediterranean; millions died. In 1835 the Medical College was founded in Calcutta, one of the oldest in Asia teaching modern medicine. Its teacher Madhusudan Gupta is remembered as the first Indian to perform a dissection there.
company.medicine.kid: A deadly disease called cholera spread from Bengal across the world in 1817. In 1835 a college opened in Calcutta to train doctors in modern medicine.

company.technology.text: Steam and wire arrived in the Company's last years. The telegraph was first installed in 1851 and a line across India was completed three years later. The first passenger railway opened in 1853, its train hauled by three steam locomotives. The Ganges Canal was finished in 1854.
company.technology.kid: In just a few years India got its first telegraph line, its first railway and a giant canal.

company.religion.text: Religion became a field of contest and reform. In Portuguese Goa an Inquisition enforced Catholic orthodoxy. At Danish Serampore, Baptist missionaries printed Bible translations in twenty-five Indian languages. In 1829 the Governor-General, Lord William Bentinck, made sati, the burning of a Hindu widow, illegal.
company.religion.kid: Christian missionaries came to India and printed the Bible in many Indian languages. In 1829 the cruel custom of burning widows was banned.

company.arts.text: Indian artists, many working for European patrons, created the Company style, a hybrid of Indian miniature tradition and European taste that began in Murshidabad and spread to Calcutta, Madras, Delhi and Lucknow. From the late 18th century the Bengal Renaissance brought a cultural, social, intellectual and artistic movement.
company.arts.kid: Indian painters mixed Indian and European ways of painting to make a new style. In Bengal, writers, artists and thinkers began an exciting movement of new ideas.

company.language.text: Fort William College, founded in Calcutta on 18 August 1800, was an academy of oriental studies. The Serampore press published a Bengali Gospel in 1800 and went on to print in many Indian languages. In 1835 the English Education Act moved the Company's education funds away from the limited support it had given to Sanskrit and Persian learning.
company.language.kid: Printing presses began to print books in Bengali and other Indian languages. In 1835 the government decided to spend its school money in a new way, and less on the old Sanskrit and Persian schools.

company.nature.text: Nature was studied and put to work. Robert Kyd proposed a botanic garden at Calcutta in 1786, matching the Company's interest in raising farm output and cash crops. The Hortus Malabaricus described the flora of the Malabar coast and its medicinal uses. Canals turned the Ganges onto the fields of the Doab.
company.nature.kid: The Company set up a botanic garden near Calcutta to find useful plants to grow and sell. A river was turned into a canal to water the fields.

sources.title: Acharya Jagadish Chandra Bose Indian Botanic Garden

company.movement.text: Europeans came by sea: the Portuguese founded their State of India seven years after Vasco da Gama found the sea route, and the Danes held Serampore. Indians were carried outward: indentured labour created a large Indian diaspora in the Caribbean, Natal, Réunion and elsewhere.
company.movement.kid: People from Portugal, Britain and other parts of Europe sailed to India. And many Indians were taken across the oceans to work, which is why Indian families live in the Caribbean and South Africa today.

company.women.text: Savitribai Phule (1831–1897) is widely regarded as the first Indian woman teacher. In 1848, with Jyotirao Phule and Sagunabai Kshirsagar, she opened the first school for girls at Bhide Wada in Pune, teaching mathematics, science and social studies despite strong opposition. Sati had been outlawed in 1829.
company.women.kid: Savitribai Phule became India's first woman teacher. In 1848 she helped to open a school for girls in Pune, even though many people were against it.

raj.power.text: From 1858 to 1947 the British Crown ruled India directly. The region included British India, administered by Britain, and the princely states, ruled by Indian princes under British paramountcy. Imperial assemblies called Delhi Durbars marked the accession of an Emperor or Empress of India. A census began in 1872.
raj.power.kid: After 1858, India was ruled by the British king or queen. Some parts were governed directly by the British, and others by Indian princes who had to obey them.

raj.war.text: Indian soldiers fought Britain's wars. In the First World War more than one million Indian troops served overseas and more than 60,000 died. In the Second, the Indian Army grew from under 200,000 men in 1939 to over 2.5 million, the largest volunteer army in history, fighting in Africa, Europe and Asia.
raj.war.kid: More than a million Indian soldiers fought in the First World War. In the Second World War, two and a half million joined up, the biggest volunteer army ever.

sources.title: Indian Army during World War I
Indian Army during World War II

raj.trade.text: Railways, roads, canals and telegraph lines were built rapidly so that raw materials such as cotton could be carried from India's hinterland to its ports more efficiently. Dadabhai Naoroji, elected to the British House of Commons in 1892, formulated the "drain theory": that economic exploitation under British rule transferred wealth from India to Britain.
raj.trade.kid: The British built railways to carry cotton and other goods to the ports. An Indian leader, Dadabhai Naoroji, argued that India's wealth was being drained away to Britain.

raj.work.text: New kinds of work appeared. The Tata Iron and Steel Company was established at Jamshedpur in 1907 and began producing steel in 1912. In western Punjab, canals opened arid land to farming, and over one million Punjabis settled in the new canal colonies.
raj.work.kid: India's first big steelworks opened at Jamshedpur. In the Punjab, more than a million people moved to farm new land watered by canals.

raj.food.text: The later 19th century saw a rise in large-scale famines, together causing deaths in the tens of millions. The Great Famine of 1876–1878 began with drought in the Deccan; a careful recent estimate puts its toll at 8.2 million. In the Bengal famine of 1943, an estimated 800,000 to 3.8 million people died.
raj.food.kid: Terrible famines struck India under British rule. Millions of people died in the famine of 1876 to 1878, and millions more in Bengal in 1943.

raj.daily.text: Cricket, first recorded in India in 1721, took root: the first first-class match was played in 1864 between Calcutta and Madras. In 1913 Dadasaheb Phalke made Raja Harishchandra, often considered the first full-length Indian feature film. Passenger railways spread from 1853 onward.
raj.daily.kid: People began to play and watch cricket, to travel by train and, from 1913, to go to the cinema to see Indian films.

raj.science.text: Indian scientists won world standing. C. V. Raman received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1930 for his work on the scattering of light. Jagadish Chandra Bose pioneered the study of radio microwaves and made major contributions to botany. Srinivasa Ramanujan (1887–1920) made substantial contributions to number theory and infinite series. The Indian Institute of Science opened in 1909.
raj.science.kid: The physicist C. V. Raman won a Nobel Prize in 1930 for discovering something new about light. Ramanujan, a brilliant mathematician, did great work with numbers in his short life.

raj.medicine.text: Bubonic plague reached Bombay in 1896, part of the third plague pandemic; the bacteriologist Waldemar Haffkine did pioneering work on vaccines. In 1897 Ronald Ross found the malaria parasite in a mosquito, proving how the disease spreads. In 1922 Upendranath Brahmachari synthesised urea-stibamine, an effective treatment for kala-azar.
raj.medicine.kid: In India in 1897, a doctor proved that mosquitoes spread malaria. An Indian scientist, Upendranath Brahmachari, discovered a medicine for a deadly fever called kala-azar.

raj.technology.text: Railways, roads, canals, bridges and telegraph links were rapidly built across India in the decades after 1858. Heavy industry followed: the Tata works began making pig iron in 1911 and steel in 1912.
raj.technology.kid: Railways, bridges, canals and telegraph lines spread across India. In 1912 India began to make its own steel.

raj.religion.text: Reform movements reshaped the religions. Dayananda Saraswati founded the Arya Samaj in the 1870s, grounded in the authority of the Vedas. Swami Vivekananda spoke at the Parliament of the World's Religions in Chicago in 1893. The Aligarh Movement, around the college founded in 1875, promoted modern scientific education for Muslims.
raj.religion.kid: Religious teachers tried to renew their faiths. Swami Vivekananda travelled to America in 1893 and gave a famous speech about Hinduism. At Aligarh, a new college taught modern science to Muslim students.

raj.arts.text: Raja Ravi Varma (1848–1906) fused European academic painting with Indian subjects. The Bengal School of Art began in Calcutta and Shantiniketan and spread across the subcontinent. In 1913 Rabindranath Tagore became the first non-European to win a Nobel Prize, and the first Indian feature film was released.
raj.arts.kid: The poet Rabindranath Tagore won the Nobel Prize in 1913. The painter Raja Ravi Varma mixed European and Indian ways of painting, and the first Indian films were made.

raj.language.text: The Linguistic Survey of India, proposed by George Grierson, formally began in 1894 and published its last results in 1928; it described 364 languages and dialects of British India. Writers such as Tagore, who wrote in Bengali, built modern literatures in the Indian languages.
raj.language.kid: A great survey counted and described 364 languages and dialects spoken in India. Writers like Tagore wrote wonderful books in their own languages.

raj.nature.text: The land was transformed and, here and there, protected. Canals brought arid western Punjab under cultivation. Kaziranga in Assam, beside the Brahmaputra and home to the Indian rhinoceros, was first set aside in 1905. Drought remained deadly: the famine of 1876 followed an intense drought in the Deccan.
raj.nature.kid: Canals turned dry land in the Punjab into farms. In Assam, land that is home to the Indian rhinoceros was first protected in 1905. It is now Kaziranga National Park.

raj.movement.text: People moved in great numbers: over a million Punjabis to the canal colonies, and more than a million soldiers overseas in the First World War. Others travelled to learn and to teach, like Anandibai Joshi, who went abroad to study medicine, and Vivekananda, who went to the United States in 1893.
raj.movement.kid: Millions of Indians moved to new farms, sailed abroad as soldiers, or travelled to study in other countries.

sources.title: Indian Army during World War I

raj.women.text: Pandita Ramabai (1858–1922) founded Sharada Sadan, a home of learning for child widows. Anandibai Joshi (1865–1887) became the first certified Indian woman doctor of western medicine, and Kadambini Ganguly the first to practise. Begum Rokeya wrote and taught for women's education in Bengal. In 1891 the age of consent was raised from ten to twelve.
raj.women.kid: Brave women opened new doors. Anandibai Joshi became one of India's first women doctors. Pandita Ramabai opened a home and school for young widows, and Begum Rokeya fought for girls' education.

independence.power.text: The Indian National Congress, founded on 28 December 1885, was the first modern nationalist movement of its kind; the All-India Muslim League, active from 1906, spoke for Muslim interests. Gandhi launched the non-cooperation movement on 4 September 1920. The Government of India Act 1935 gave the provinces a greater measure of autonomy.
independence.power.kid: Indians formed political parties to ask for a say in their own government, and then for freedom. Under Gandhi's leadership, many people refused to cooperate with British rule.

independence.war.text: On 13 April 1919 Brigadier-General Dyer blocked the exit of the Jallianwala Bagh in Amritsar and ordered his troops to fire on the crowd. Some nationalists took up arms: revolutionaries raided the Chittagong armoury on 18 April 1930, and during the Second World War the Indian National Army, allied with Japan, joined an invasion that was halted at Imphal.
independence.war.kid: In 1919 soldiers under a British general fired on a large crowd gathered in a garden in Amritsar. Most Indians followed Gandhi's peaceful way, but some took up weapons to fight for freedom.

independence.trade.text: Buying and selling became weapons. The Swadeshi movement, formally launched at Calcutta's Town Hall on 7 August 1905, aimed to curb foreign goods by relying on domestic production, and the boycott of foreign cloth stayed prominent. In 1930 Gandhi's Salt March challenged the British monopoly on salt.
independence.trade.kid: Indians stopped buying British cloth and made their own instead. In 1930 Gandhi walked to the sea to make salt, because the British would not let Indians make or sell it freely.

independence.work.text: Workers and peasants entered politics. At Champaran in 1917, Gandhi's first satyagraha in India backed farmers forced to grow indigo for barely any payment. The All India Trade Union Congress was founded on 31 October 1920 with Lala Lajpat Rai as its first president. Gandhi urged Indians to spin their own yarn on the charkha.
independence.work.kid: Gandhi's first big protest in India was for poor farmers who were forced to grow indigo for almost no pay. Factory workers formed trade unions to ask for fair treatment.

independence.food.text: Food and tax were bound together. At Kheda in 1918, Gandhi organised support for peasants who could not pay land revenue because of famine and plague. The Salt March of 1930 was a campaign of tax resistance against the British salt monopoly: 24 days and 387 kilometres on foot from Sabarmati Ashram to Dandi.
independence.food.kid: Everyone needs salt, and the British taxed it. So in 1930 Gandhi walked 387 kilometres to the sea in protest. Earlier, he had helped farmers who could not pay their taxes after a famine.

independence.daily.text: Nationalism reached into everyday life. Gandhi promoted khadi, hand-spun and hand-woven cloth, as swadeshi, of the homeland. "Vande Mataram", adopted by the Congress in 1905, became a salutation to the motherland. Crowds shouted "Inquilab Zindabad", Hindustani for "Long live the revolution".
independence.daily.kid: People showed they wanted freedom in their daily lives. They wore khadi, cloth spun and woven by hand at home. They sang "Vande Mataram" and shouted "Long live the revolution!"

independence.science.text: Indian science grew in these same decades. Jagadish Chandra Bose founded the Bose Institute on 30 November 1917. In the early 1920s Satyendra Nath Bose laid the foundation of Bose–Einstein statistics; the particles called bosons are named after him. Meghnad Saha's ionisation equation let astronomers relate the spectra of stars to their temperatures.
independence.science.kid: Indian scientists made great discoveries in these years. A whole family of tiny particles, the bosons, is named after the physicist Satyendra Nath Bose.

independence.medicine.text: The chemist Prafulla Chandra Ray founded Bengal Chemical in Calcutta in 1901 to make chemicals and medicines in India; it survives as a government-owned pharmaceutical maker. In 1943 the government set up the Bhore Committee to survey the country's health conditions and health organisation; its report came in 1946.
independence.medicine.kid: An Indian chemist, Prafulla Chandra Ray, started a company in 1901 to make medicines in India. Just before independence, a committee studied the health of the whole country.

independence.technology.text: Old and new technologies both served the cause. Gandhi made the hand spinning wheel a symbol, and in Hind Swaraj set out his doubts about mechanisation. Yet during the Quit India Movement an underground station, Congress Radio, organised by the 22-year-old student Usha Mehta, broadcast from 27 August to 12 November 1942.
independence.technology.kid: Gandhi chose the simple spinning wheel as the sign of freedom. But a young student named Usha Mehta used a secret radio station to spread news of the freedom struggle in 1942.

sources.title: Hind Swaraj or Indian Home Rule

independence.religion.text: Religion and caste ran through the freedom struggle. The Khilafat movement of 1919–1922 mobilised Muslims over the fate of the Ottoman caliphate. At Vaikom in 1924–25, protesters demanded access to the roads around a temple; at Mahad on 20 March 1927, B. R. Ambedkar led Dalits to drink from a public tank. The Poona Pact of 1932 raised the political representation of the depressed classes.
independence.religion.kid: The freedom movement was also a fight for fairness between Indians. B. R. Ambedkar led people who were called "untouchable" to drink from a public water tank that had been forbidden to them.

independence.arts.text: Artists gave the nation a face and a voice. Abanindranath Tagore painted Bharat Mata, "Mother India", in watercolour in 1905; he had first called it "Mother Bengal". Bankim Chandra Chatterjee's poem "Vande Mataram", published in his novel Anandamath in 1882, was sung as an ode to the motherland. Sarojini Naidu was both poet and political leader.
independence.arts.kid: An artist painted India as a mother, and a poem called "Vande Mataram" praised the motherland. Songs, poems and pictures helped people to feel they belonged to one country.

independence.language.text: The movement spoke in India's own languages. Gandhi wrote Hind Swaraj in 1909 in Gujarati, his mother tongue; the government banned it in 1910 as seditious. "Vande Mataram" was written in Bengali. The slogan "Inquilab Zindabad" is Hindustani.
independence.language.kid: Gandhi wrote his ideas about freedom in his own language, Gujarati, and the British banned the book. Songs and slogans in Bengali and Hindustani spread across the country.

sources.title: Hind Swaraj or Indian Home Rule

independence.nature.text: Famine and plague stood behind the peasants' protest at Kheda in 1918. Nationalists began to plan for the land itself: the astrophysicist Meghnad Saha campaigned for river valley development and flood control. And the Salt March ended on the shore at Dandi.
independence.nature.kid: Floods, droughts and disease made life hard for farmers, and helped to push them to protest. Indian scientists began to plan how to control the rivers.

independence.movement.text: The struggle was carried by Indians abroad as well as at home. Gandhi returned from South Africa in 1915. Expatriate Indians founded the Ghadar movement to overthrow British rule. On 23 May 1914 the passengers of the steamship Komagata Maru were denied entry at Vancouver. The Indian National Army was formed in Southeast Asia.
independence.movement.kid: Indians living in other countries joined the fight for freedom too. Gandhi himself came home from South Africa in 1915 with new ideas about peaceful protest.

independence.women.text: Women were leaders of the movement. Sarojini Naidu was a poet and political activist. Aruna Asaf Ali hoisted the national flag at Gowalia Tank Maidan in Bombay in 1942. Rani Gaidinliu, a Naga leader, was arrested in 1932 at 16 and sentenced to life imprisonment. Matangini Hazra, born in 1870, died on 29 September 1942 while leading a batch of volunteers.
independence.women.kid: Many women were leaders in the freedom struggle. Aruna Asaf Ali raised the Indian flag in Bombay in 1942. Rani Gaidinliu led a revolt in the Naga hills when she was only a teenager.

partition.power.text: The Indian Independence Act 1947 partitioned British India into two dominions, India and Pakistan. The 562 princely states then had to be brought in; Vallabhbhai Patel and V. P. Menon carried out their integration into India. The Constituent Assembly adopted the constitution on 26 November 1949, and it came into force on 26 January 1950.
partition.power.kid: In August 1947 British rule ended and two new countries were born: India and Pakistan. Hundreds of small kingdoms joined them. India then wrote its own constitution.

partition.war.text: Violence came before and after the border. Direct Action Day, 16 August 1946, led to the great Calcutta riots. From 1947 to 1948 India and Pakistan fought their first war, over the princely state of Jammu and Kashmir. In September 1948 a military operation called a "police action" annexed Hyderabad to India.
partition.war.kid: The new countries were born in fighting. There were terrible riots, and India and Pakistan went to war over Kashmir in their very first year.

partition.trade.text: The new border cut through working economies. In Bengal the fertile east had produced food and raw materials for the industrial west, which sent back manufactured goods. Partition left all the coal mines and all but two of the jute mills on the western side, a division foreseen as economically disastrous for East Bengal.
partition.trade.kid: The new border cut across old trade routes. In Bengal, the farms that grew raw materials ended up in one country and almost all the jute mills in the other.

partition.work.text: Millions of refugees had to rebuild their working lives. After 1947, under the leadership of Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay, over 50,000 refugees were resettled at Faridabad near Delhi, reviving the city's economy and social life.
partition.work.kid: People who had lost their homes and jobs had to start again. More than 50,000 refugees were given a new start in the town of Faridabad, near Delhi.

partition.food.text: Partition separated people from their food supply. After 1947 West Bengal suffered a substantial food shortage, because the fertile rice-growing districts had gone to East Bengal.
partition.food.kid: After the border was drawn, West Bengal did not have enough food, because the best rice fields were now on the other side.

partition.daily.text: For millions, daily life became life in a camp. Kingsway Camp in north Delhi became the city's largest refugee camp, sheltering 300,000 people. In all, Partition displaced between 12 and 20 million people along religious lines.
partition.daily.kid: Millions of families had to leave their homes and live in camps. One camp in Delhi held 300,000 people.

partition.science.text: Even amid the upheaval, the foundations of national science were laid. The Council of Scientific and Industrial Research had been set up in 1942, and the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research, proposed by Homi Bhabha, was founded in 1945. The Atomic Energy Commission was established on 3 August 1948.
partition.science.kid: Even in these hard years, India set up new places for science. In 1948 it created a commission to study the energy inside atoms.

sources.title: Council of Scientific and Industrial Research

partition.medicine.text: Rajkumari Amrit Kaur became independent India's first Health Minister in 1947 and held the post until 1957. The new government inherited the Bhore Committee's 1946 survey of the country's health conditions.
partition.medicine.kid: India's first Health Minister was a woman, Rajkumari Amrit Kaur. She looked after the country's health for ten years.

partition.technology.text: The new state turned at once to large projects. The Damodar Valley Project, begun after the devastating flood of 1943 in a flood-prone valley, was the first multipurpose river valley project of independent India; the astrophysicist Meghnad Saha was a pioneer in conceiving and advocating it.
partition.technology.kid: One of free India's first big projects was to tame the river Damodar with dams, to stop floods and make electricity.

partition.religion.text: Partition divided people along religious lines, with large-scale violence between communities, as at Noakhali in Bengal in 1946, where Hindus were massacred. On 30 January 1948 Mahatma Gandhi, aged 78, was shot dead in New Delhi by Nathuram Godse, a Hindu nationalist.
partition.religion.kid: The border was drawn by religion, and people of different religions attacked one another. In January 1948 Gandhi was shot dead in New Delhi.

partition.arts.text: Writers recorded what official papers could not. Amrita Pritam's poem "Ajj aakhaan Waris Shah nu" voiced her anguish at the massacres. Saadat Hasan Manto's story "Toba Tek Singh", published in 1955, follows the inmates of a Lahore asylum who are to be divided between the two countries. Khushwant Singh's novel Train to Pakistan, 1956, sees Partition from one border village.
partition.arts.kid: Writers told the story of Partition in poems, stories and novels. They showed how ordinary people suffered when the border was drawn.

partition.language.text: Language soon became a new fault line. In 1948 the government of Pakistan ordained that Urdu would be the sole federal language. In East Bengal a movement arose for the recognition of Bengali, reaching its height in 1952. Partition's own literature was written in several languages: Manto wrote in Urdu, Amrita Pritam in Punjabi and Hindi.
partition.language.kid: Pakistan's leaders said that Urdu would be the only national language. But people in East Bengal spoke Bengali, and they protested to defend their language.

partition.nature.text: The Radcliffe Line divided 175,000 square miles of land, and with it rivers and canals. In the first years after Partition the waters of the Indus system were shared out under an Inter-Dominion Accord of 4 May 1948, until the Indus Waters Treaty of 1960.
partition.nature.kid: The new border cut across rivers and canals. India and Pakistan had to agree how to share the water of the river Indus.

partition.movement.text: Partition displaced between 12 and 20 million people and created overwhelming refugee crises. New towns grew to hold them. With Lahore lost to Pakistan, East Punjab needed a new capital, and Chandigarh was founded in the aftermath.
partition.movement.kid: Between 12 and 20 million people left their homes and crossed the new border. New towns were built for them.

partition.women.text: Women suffered Partition's violence in particular ways: it is estimated that between 75,000 and 100,000 women were kidnapped and raped. The Liaquat–Nehru Pact later provided that abducted women were to be returned. Women also helped to found the republic: Amrit Kaur sat in the Constituent Assembly and became a minister.
partition.women.kid: Partition was especially cruel to women, and many thousands were kidnapped. Women also helped to build the new country: some helped to write India's constitution.

sources.title: Violence against women during the Partition of India

republic.power.text: India's first general elections ran from 25 October 1951 to 21 February 1952 with 173 million registered voters, the largest election held up to that time. In 1956 the states were redrawn along linguistic lines. From 1975 to 1977 Indira Gandhi ruled by decree under a state of emergency: civil liberties were suspended and most opponents imprisoned.
republic.power.kid: In 1951 and 1952, India held its first election, the biggest the world had ever seen. Later, for 21 months in the 1970s, the prime minister took emergency powers and put her opponents in prison.

republic.war.text: India fought China along the disputed Himalayan border in October and November 1962. In 1971 it joined the Bangladesh Liberation War on 3 December, after Pakistani air strikes and the flight of some 10 million refugees from East Pakistan. In Sri Lanka, civil war began on 23 July 1983.
republic.war.kid: India fought a short war with China in 1962. In 1971 it helped Bangladesh to win its freedom from Pakistan. In Sri Lanka, a long civil war began in 1983.

republic.trade.text: From 1951 India's economy was steered by Five-Year Plans, inspired by the Soviet model, aiming at balanced growth and less poverty. Industry operated under what C. Rajagopalachari named the "Licence Raj", a system of strict government control and regulation.
republic.trade.kid: The government planned the economy five years at a time. A business needed many official permits before it could make or sell anything.

republic.work.text: The state built heavy industry, such as the Bhilai Steel Plant, India's first and main producer of steel rails. On 18 January 1982 the mill workers of Bombay began a great strike for a bonus and higher wages. In Ahmedabad, self-employed women formed their own union, SEWA, in 1972.
republic.work.kid: The government built big steelworks that gave many people jobs. In Bombay, the cloth-mill workers went on strike in 1982 for better pay.

republic.food.text: The Green Revolution, from the 1960s, brought high-yielding crop varieties and fertilisers; in India it was led by M. S. Swaminathan as part of Norman Borlaug's wider effort. Operation Flood, launched on 13 January 1970, was the world's largest dairy development programme and turned a milk-deficient India into the world's largest milk producer.
republic.food.kid: New kinds of crops and fertilisers gave much bigger harvests. A dairy programme that began in 1970 made India the world's biggest producer of milk.

republic.daily.text: Television arrived with the state broadcaster Doordarshan, established on 15 September 1959. From 1983 the small Maruti 800 city car was on sale. In June 1983 India won the Cricket World Cup in England. Films such as Sholay, released in 1975, were shared experiences.
republic.daily.kid: Families began to watch television, and a small car called the Maruti 800 appeared on the roads. In 1983 India won the Cricket World Cup.

republic.science.text: India built national programmes in atomic energy and space. It conducted its first nuclear test at Pokhran on 18 May 1974. Its first satellite, Aryabhata, was launched on a Soviet rocket on 19 April 1975. On 3 April 1984 Rakesh Sharma became the first Indian in space, aboard Soyuz T-11.
republic.science.kid: India launched its first satellite in 1975 and named it after the ancient astronomer Aryabhata. In 1984 Rakesh Sharma became the first Indian to travel into space.

republic.medicine.text: The All India Institute of Medical Sciences in Delhi was set up under an Act of 1956. Smallpox, which still circulated in India in 1967, was wiped out: the world's last natural case was in 1977. On 3 December 1984, gas from a pesticide plant in Bhopal reached over 500,000 people, in what is considered the world's worst industrial disaster.
republic.medicine.kid: India built new hospitals and medical colleges, and smallpox, a terrible disease, was wiped out everywhere. But in 1984 poison gas leaked from a factory in Bhopal and harmed a huge number of people.

sources.title: All India Institute of Medical Sciences, Delhi

republic.technology.text: Big dams were the emblem of the new India. The Bhakra Dam, a concrete gravity dam 226 metres high on the Satluj, was called the "New Temple of Resurgent India" by Jawaharlal Nehru. Television had begun in 1959, and the first satellite followed in 1975.
republic.technology.kid: India built giant dams to store water. The Bhakra Dam is 226 metres high. The first prime minister called it a temple of the new India.

republic.religion.text: In the 1950s the Hindu code bills codified and reformed Hindu personal law. In 1956 B. R. Ambedkar and nearly half a million Dalits converted to Navayana Buddhism. In June 1984 the army's Operation Blue Star removed armed militants from the Golden Temple complex in Amritsar.
republic.religion.kid: In 1956 B. R. Ambedkar and almost half a million Dalits became Buddhists.

republic.arts.text: Satyajit Ray's first film, Pather Panchali (1955), adapted a Bengali novel. Popular Hindi cinema produced films such as the action-adventure Sholay (1975). The sitar virtuoso Ravi Shankar made Indian classical music better known in the West in the 1960s through his teaching, performances and association with Yehudi Menuhin and George Harrison.
republic.arts.kid: Indian films became famous, from Satyajit Ray's Pather Panchali to the action film Sholay. The sitar player Ravi Shankar took Indian music around the world.

republic.language.text: Language shaped the map. The States Reorganisation Act of 1956 redrew India's states along linguistic lines. Tamil Nadu saw mass protests against the imposition of Hindi. In Ceylon, the 1956 act known as "Sinhala Only" replaced English with Sinhala as the sole official language.
republic.language.kid: India's states were redrawn so that people who speak the same language live in the same state. People in Tamil Nadu protested against being made to use Hindi.

republic.nature.text: In 1973 the government began Project Tiger to protect the endangered tiger. In the same decade the Chipko movement's villagers hugged trees to stop commercial logging. Nature could be merciless: the Bhola cyclone of 1970 killed at least 300,000 people in the Ganges delta, the deadliest tropical cyclone on record.
republic.nature.kid: In the 1970s villagers hugged trees to stop them being cut down, and India began to protect its tigers. In 1970 a giant storm killed at least 300,000 people in what is now Bangladesh.

republic.movement.text: Refugees crossed South Asia's new borders. During the Lhasa uprising of March 1959 the Dalai Lama escaped to India. In 1971 some 10 million people fled East Pakistan into the Indian state of West Bengal and its neighbours.
republic.movement.kid: In 1959 the Dalai Lama escaped from Tibet to India. In 1971 about ten million people fled to India from the war in what became Bangladesh.

republic.women.text: Sirimavo Bandaranaike of Sri Lanka became the world's first woman prime minister in 1960; Indira Gandhi led India from 1966 to 1977 and from 1980 to 1984. The Hindu Succession Act of 1956 gave a Hindu woman absolute ownership of her property. Ela Bhatt founded SEWA, a union of self-employed women, in 1972, and women were the backbone of Chipko.
republic.women.kid: Sri Lanka had the world's first woman prime minister, and India soon had Indira Gandhi. Poor working women formed their own union, and village women led the fight to save forests.

since-1991.power.text: From 1991 India opened its economy and gave markets a larger role. The Seventy-third Amendment of 1992 gave village councils constitutional status, with elections every five years and reserved seats. The Right to Information Act of 2005 set out citizens' right to see official records. Elsewhere in the region, the Taliban captured Kabul on 15 August 2021.
since-1991.power.kid: Since 1991 India has changed quickly. Villages elect their own councils, and citizens have the right to ask the government for information.

sources.title: Seventy-third Amendment of the Constitution of India

since-1991.war.text: India tested five nuclear devices at Pokhran in May 1998. From May to July 1999 it fought Pakistan in the Kargil district of Ladakh. In November 2008 ten members of Lashkar-e-Taiba attacked Mumbai. Sri Lanka's 26-year civil war ended in May 2009, and the war in Afghanistan with the fall of Kabul in 2021.
since-1991.war.kid: India and Pakistan fought a short war in the mountains at Kargil in 1999. Sri Lanka's long civil war ended in 2009.

since-1991.trade.text: The reforms that began in 1991 opened India to foreign trade and investment. Information technology services became a leading export: the sector contributes about 7.5 per cent of GDP, with exports of $224 billion in the 2025 financial year. On 1 July 2017 a single Goods and Services Tax replaced several older taxes.
since-1991.trade.kid: After 1991 India began to trade much more with the world. Its computer and software companies now sell their services to customers everywhere.

since-1991.work.text: New work appeared in offices: the IT sector employs nearly six million people directly. In the countryside, a 2005 act aimed to guarantee a "right to work". In Bangladesh, the Rana Plaza building, which housed five garment factories, collapsed on 24 April 2013, killing 1,134 people: the deadliest garment-factory disaster in history.
since-1991.work.kid: Millions of Indians now work with computers. In villages, a law promises paid work to people who need it. In Bangladesh, a building full of clothing factories collapsed in 2013, and more than a thousand workers died.

sources.title: Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act, 2005

since-1991.food.text: The National Food Security Act of 2013 aims to provide subsidised food grains to about two thirds of India's people. Farming remains political: in 2020 and 2021, tens of thousands of farmers marched towards Delhi in protest against three new farm acts.
since-1991.food.kid: A law of 2013 says that about two out of three Indians can buy grain at a low price. In 2020 farmers marched to Delhi to protest against new farm laws.

since-1991.daily.text: Daily life went digital. Jio's mobile network opened to the public on 5 September 2016. The Unified Payments Interface, launched the same year, handles over 250 billion transactions a year, about half the world's digital transactions. The Indian Premier League began in April 2008, and Delhi's Metro opened its first section on 25 December 2002.
since-1991.daily.kid: Today many Indians pay for things with their phones. People watch IPL cricket and ride metro trains in the big cities.

since-1991.science.text: Chandrayaan-1, India's first lunar probe, launched in October 2008, discovered water molecules widely present in lunar soil. The Mars Orbiter Mission reached Mars orbit on 24 September 2014, making India the first Asian nation to do so. On 23 August 2023 Chandrayaan-3 touched down near the Moon's south pole.
since-1991.science.kid: India has sent spacecraft to the Moon and to Mars. In 2023 its lander touched down near the Moon's south pole.

since-1991.medicine.text: The Pulse Polio campaign vaccinated all children under five; India's last wild polio cases were reported on 13 January 2011, and the WHO declared the country polio-free on 27 March 2014. India is often described as the "pharmacy of the world". In the COVID-19 pandemic it reported 45 million cases and developed its own vaccine, Covaxin.
since-1991.medicine.kid: India beat polio by vaccinating every young child, and has been free of the disease since 2014. Indian factories make medicines for the whole world.

since-1991.technology.text: India built digital systems at vast scale: Aadhaar, a twelve-digit identity number based on biometric and demographic data, and UPI, an instant payment system. On the ground, the Golden Quadrilateral highways link Delhi, Kolkata, Mumbai and Chennai, and construction of the Delhi Metro began in 1998.
since-1991.technology.kid: India has built new highways between its biggest cities and metro railways inside them. People can get a twelve-digit identity number called Aadhaar.

since-1991.religion.text: Religious identity has been a source of conflict in this period. On 6 December 1992 the Babri Masjid, a 16th-century mosque in Ayodhya long the subject of dispute, was destroyed by a large group of activists of the Vishva Hindu Parishad and allied organisations. In March 2001 the Taliban destroyed the two monumental Buddhas of Bamiyan in Afghanistan.
since-1991.religion.kid: Arguments about religion have sometimes turned violent. In 1992 a crowd pulled down an old mosque in Ayodhya. In 2001 the Taliban blew up two giant ancient statues of the Buddha in Afghanistan.

since-1991.arts.text: Indian artists reached world audiences. The composer A. R. Rahman, known for his work in Indian cinema, has won two Academy Awards and two Grammy Awards. Arundhati Roy's first novel, The God of Small Things, won the Booker Prize in 1997.
since-1991.arts.kid: The composer A. R. Rahman won two Oscars for his film music. The writer Arundhati Roy won a famous prize for her first novel.

since-1991.language.text: In 2004 the government created the status of "classical language"; Tamil was the first to be recognised, and by 2024 there were eleven. The People's Linguistic Survey of India, launched in 2010, identified 780 languages in the country.
since-1991.language.kid: A survey that began in 2010 found 780 different languages in India. Eleven very old languages, starting with Tamil, have been named "classical languages".

since-1991.nature.text: The plates that built the Himalaya still move. An earthquake struck Kutch in Gujarat on 26 January 2001. On 26 December 2004 a magnitude 9.2–9.3 rupture between the Burma and Indian plates sent a tsunami across the Indian Ocean. The Nepal earthquake of April 2015 killed 8,962 people. A newer danger is man-made: Delhi's air was found to be among the most lethal of 7,000 world cities.
since-1991.nature.kid: Great earthquakes struck Gujarat in 2001 and Nepal in 2015, and in 2004 an undersea earthquake sent giant waves across the Indian Ocean. Dirty air in big cities is a newer danger.

since-1991.movement.text: By a government report of November 2024, 35.4 million non-resident Indians and people of Indian origin live outside India. The region also shelters people in flight: by the UN refugee agency's count, more than 723,000 Rohingya have fled from Myanmar to Bangladesh.
since-1991.movement.kid: More than 35 million people from Indian families now live in other countries. And hundreds of thousands of Rohingya people have fled from Myanmar to camps in Bangladesh.

since-1991.women.text: The Seventy-third Amendment reserved seats for women in village councils; an amendment of 2023 seeks to reserve 33 per cent of seats in the Lok Sabha and state assemblies. Droupadi Murmu, president since 2022, is the first from a tribal community and the second woman in the office. Malala Yousafzai of Pakistan won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2014 at 17. The gang rape and murder of a 22-year-old woman in Delhi in December 2012 is known as the Nirbhaya case.
since-1991.women.kid: Seats are kept for women on every village council. Droupadi Murmu became India's president in 2022, the first from an Adivasi community. Malala Yousafzai of Pakistan won the Nobel Peace Prize when she was only 17, for standing up for girls' education.
